b0a9a999ad0d7d069578aa850d61e50d8ffd15ce.content:
Concilium started as a weekend project and turned into something people actually rely on. The tool helps developers manage configuration files across multiple environments. The problem was one I encountered repeatedly. The solution was straightforward. The process of turning a personal utility into a maintained open source tool taught me about documentation, issue triage, and community management. Skills that are not about coding at all.

#Concilium #build #opensource #tech #coding #development #utiltity #maintenance #community #learning #experience #innovation

36f081106a02b5307523523a2016c526d5d20240.content:
The best feature of Concilium came from a user suggestion. I had not thought of it. The user had a specific need that my tool did not meet. They described the problem clearly. I built the feature in a weekend. The result was better than anything I would have designed alone. Open source development with user input produces better outcomes than isolated development. The collaboration makes the product better.

#Concilium #opensource #collaboration #tech #coding #development #feedback #feature #community #user #input #improvement

69d25bd962c1c7e5601d583d68f85191ad57c5fa.content:
Maintaining Concilium has been harder than building it. The initial development took two weeks. The ongoing maintenance takes a few hours every week. Bug fixes. Compatibility updates. Documentation improvements. The maintenance burden is real and underestimated by new developers. Building something is fun. Maintaining something is work. The projects that survive are the ones where the maintainer accepts the maintenance as part of the commitment.

#Concilium #maintenance #opensource #tech #coding #development #commitment #burden #reality #lesson #experience #build

a783442b04258ab80d48b413acba7bf7c2501836.content:
Concilium is not a popular tool by any metric. It has a few hundred users. But those users depend on it. When I pushed a breaking change without proper notice, several people reached out frustrated. I learned to be more careful. The lesson is that even small tools have users who rely on them. The responsibility of maintaining something other people depend on is real, regardless of the project size.

#Concilium #responsibility #opensource #tech #coding #development #dependability #lesson #experience #users #maintenance #commitment

fa8ff31488410e0d17128bb06e256d497f8cb07a.content:
The Thinker was my attempt to build an AI agent that could reason through problems step by step. The concept was simple. Feed it a problem. Let it think out loud. Get a solution. The implementation was more complex than I expected. The challenge was not the AI integration. It was the state management. Keeping track of what the agent had considered, what it had ruled out, and what it was currently exploring required careful architecture.

#TheThinker #AI #agent #build #tech #coding #development #reasoning #architecture #learning #experience #innovation

a20a050a95a2e6d6b441c892ca2733c36b8a6d45.content:
The Thinker failed in an instructive way. The agent would get stuck in loops. It would consider the same options repeatedly without making progress. The reasoning trace would grow longer without converging on a solution. The problem was not the AI capability. It was the lack of a mechanism for the agent to recognize when it was going in circles. The lesson was that reasoning requires self-monitoring, not just generation.

#TheThinker #AI #failure #lesson #tech #coding #development #reasoning #loops #monitoring #learning #experience

34beccdcb154edb2b319fb34cb3fb8eee5887be8.content:
I rebuilt The Thinker with a different architecture. The new version maintains a working memory of what has been tried and what has been ruled out. The improvement was dramatic. The agent still makes mistakes. But it does not repeat the same mistakes. The architecture of memory is as important as the architecture of reasoning. The human brain has the same property. We remember what we tried so we do not try it again.

#TheThinker #AI #architecture #memory #tech #coding #development #reasoning #improvement #lesson #learning #experience

276eb7ac8e62e1449f56a2fc12af2ad018485c08.content:
The Thinker taught me that building AI agents is more about system design than AI capability. The AI is the reasoning engine. The system around it determines whether the reasoning is effective. Prompt structure. Memory management. Error handling. Output validation. These are the components that make an agent useful. The AI is a component. The system is the product.

#TheThinker #AI #agents #systemdesign #tech #coding #development #architecture #lesson #learning #innovation #product

3f30df8106c3d405859f3e5ee95c860489b8eeb2.content:
OpenMeta was my first attempt at building something that other people could use. The code was messy. The documentation was sparse. The UX was questionable. But it worked. The experience of putting something imperfect into the world taught me that shipping beats perfection. The criticism I received was useful. The encouragement I received was motivating. The act of shipping changed my relationship with building.

#OpenMeta #build #shipping #tech #coding #development #opensource #experience #lesson #learning #perfection #growth

7c31c6f3fd025c13a67242c00216d24b721b1c6f.content:
SnapGPT was a different experience. I had learned from OpenMeta. The code was cleaner. The documentation was better. The launch was more organized. The difference was not talent. It was experience. Building one thing teaches you how to build the next thing better. The improvement is not in technical skill. It is in judgment. Knowing what matters and what does not. That is the skill that compounds.

#SnapGPT #build #improvement #tech #coding #development #opensource #experience #lesson #learning #judgment #compound

09e33a195523b4fc6b2e33e8da98f7eae77641cc.content:
The most valuable feedback I received on SnapGPT was negative. A user told me the tool was confusing to set up. I was defensive at first. I had spent hours on the setup experience. Then I watched them try to use it. They were right. The setup was confusing from a fresh perspective. I had become blind to the friction because I was too familiar with the tool. Fresh eyes see what habituated eyes miss.

#SnapGPT #feedback #negative #tech #coding #development #opensource #experience #lesson #learning #growth #freshperspective

7341f6f6a23dab8449f1afa5788fc9a5b8125285.content:
Both OpenMeta and SnapGPT have been superseded by better tools. That is fine. The point was not to build a lasting product. The point was to learn the process of building, shipping, and maintaining. The tools themselves are less important than the skills developed through creating them. The portfolio is not the product. The portfolio is the evidence of the learning.

#OpenMeta #SnapGPT #learning #build #tech #coding #development #opensource #portfolio #skills #experience #growth

c5843c0d7ef4c2a2d6f129e579a87bf8efb12b2b.content:
Building an FPS game with AI tools has been the most educational project I have attempted. The game mechanics are straightforward. The implementation details are endless. Collision detection. Weapon balancing. Enemy AI. Level design. UI. Sound. Each system is simple in isolation. The complexity comes from their interaction. The AI helps with implementation. The design requires human judgment. The combination is powerful.

#gamedev #FPS #AI #build #tech #coding #development #gaming #indiegame #learning #experience #innovation

fb1a8952bd7c94323e2a6f5c3abdbac859bb79dd.content:
The FPS project broke in a way that taught me the most. The weapon system and the enemy AI system had a subtle incompatibility. The enemy AI assumed weapons had instant hit detection. The weapon system used projectile physics. The enemies could not be hit because the AI was dodging projectiles that moved at a finite speed. The fix required understanding both systems deeply. The AI helped with the fix. But I had to understand the problem first.

#gamedev #FPS #debugging #AI #tech #coding #development #gaming #indiegame #lesson #experience #learning

45bf4ed3da3f571e805990a005ccccec9fdd9708.content:
I am not a 3D artist. I am not a sound designer. I am not an animator. AI tools let me generate placeholder assets that are good enough to test gameplay. The FPS looks rough. The sounds are generic. But the gameplay is functional. The mechanics are testable. The level flow is iterable. The AI fills the skill gaps that would have stopped me from starting. The barrier to entry for solo game development has never been lower.

#gamedev #FPS #AI #assets #tech #coding #development #gaming #indiegame #solodev #barrier #opportunity

f53999f4117bf2d09ac967835cf1062fdea5b08e.content:
LinkedIn influencer culture is exhausting. The same motivational quotes recycled by different accounts. The humble brags disguised as lessons. The relentless positivity that excludes any genuine vulnerability. The platform rewards the appearance of success more than the reality of it. The people who post about grinding and hustling are usually the ones with the least to show for it. The signal-to-noise ratio on LinkedIn is getting worse.

#LinkedIn #influencer #culture #rant #tech #socialmedia #motivation #positivity #reality #critique #noise #signal

33f577d2116f58058ae0a2bd7ab7dc82259bbe7c.content:
I unfollowed everyone who posts daily motivational content and my feed improved dramatically. The posts that remain are about actual work. Technical challenges. Business problems. Industry analysis. The difference is stark. Motivational content is designed to make you feel something so you engage. Informative content is designed to teach you something so you learn. The algorithm prefers the first. I prefer the second.

#LinkedIn #feed #curation #tech #socialmedia #motivation #content #algorithm #learning #experience #comparison #preference

8f9dba9a773abdb7c752ed4d14f4b748dc3b2e3b.content:
The LinkedIn engagement bait formula is predictable. Ask a controversial question. Share a personal story with a lesson. Post a hot take about a trending topic. The formula works because the algorithm rewards engagement. The quality of the content is secondary to the quantity of reactions. The platform is optimized for activity, not insight. The people who game the system best get the most visibility.

#LinkedIn #engagement #bait #tech #socialmedia #algorithm #formula #optimization #critique #analysis #visibility #quality

79999d299663cd246671497dfaa27f0e7727ed9e.content:
I think LinkedIn is becoming what Facebook became for an older generation. A platform for performative sharing that increasingly reflects what people want others to think about them rather than what is true. The authenticity that made professional networking valuable is being replaced by content optimized for the algorithm. The platform is still useful for specific purposes. The overall experience is declining.

#LinkedIn #Facebook #comparison #tech #socialmedia #performative #authenticity #decline #analysis #critique #usefulness #experience

679c89546de780c6c489e605f47eb0b806a08f57.content:
Tech Twitter is a race to the bottom where the hottest takes get the most engagement. Nuance is punished. Certainty is rewarded. The people who speak with the most confidence are often the ones who understand the subject the least. The platform incentives reward takes that are wrong in interesting ways over correct in boring ways. The result is a discourse that is entertaining and unreliable.

#Twitter #tech #discourse #rant #socialmedia #hot #takes #nuance #incentives #analysis #critique #reliability

c916fd90325a69baf30088cd146584505c25f70e.content:
I stopped posting hot takes on tech Twitter and started posting questions instead. The engagement dropped. The quality of responses improved. I learned more from the replies to my questions than I ever learned from the replies to my takes. The platform rewards certainty. The user benefits from curiosity. The incentives of the platform and the interests of the user are misaligned.

#Twitter #questions #curiosity #tech #socialmedia #engagement #learning #experience #comparison #analysis #incentives #alignment

61abedcfc7e203a66d330ff138bbac435dbed1d7.content:
The people who are most worth following on tech Twitter are the ones who admit when they are wrong. I respect someone who posts a correction more than someone who pretends they were right. The platform design does not encourage corrections. It encourages broadcasting. The people who use the platform for genuine learning are the minority. They are also the most valuable to follow.

The ghosting problem in tech recruiting is a symptom of a larger issue. The recruiting process treats candidates as interchangeable. The volume of applications is high. The reminder is useful.

cdb6580227e616ac2b26c75e68945218776350eb.content:
Six months ago I couldn't read a stack trace. Today I deleted a file that was doing nothing and the whole thing ran faster.

Nobody teaches you that. Tutorials teach you the happy path. The real learning is in the parts that break at 1am and the twenty minutes you spend staring at a line that looks fine.

I keep a folder of things I have broken. Not to feel bad about it. I keep it so I remember which mistakes I have already paid for. That's the point.

The list is long now. I'm not complaining. A database I dropped twice. A loop that ate an entire afternoon. A deploy that took the site down for eleven minutes while I watched.

Every one of those taught me something a course would have skipped. People ask how to start. I say build the dumbest possible version and break it on purpose. Reading about a system isn't the same as watching it fail while you're the one who caused it. That's the whole difference between knowing a tool and understanding it.

678f7f400b88b3f3939f2945413f402659ab5f81.content:
I built five small command line tools in one year and the biggest lesson wasn't about code.

It was about scope. Each one started as something reasonable. Each one grew a second feature. Then a config file. Then a plugin system that I thought about for three days and never once used.

The one that gets used every single day is forty lines long. I wrote it in an evening. It does one thing and it has never once surprised me. The fancy one has tests, docs, and a folder of dead code I keep meaning to clean up. I open it twice a month. That's it.

So the bar I use now is simple. If I can't explain the tool in one sentence, it's too big. If it needs a config file, I ask whether it needs to exist at all. Usually it doesn't. Small tools aren't less ambitious. They are just honest about how much time I actually have.

I think the industry has this backwards. Everyone brags about the size of what they built, and almost nobody brags about how little they got away with.

1cf436302dfc24b1d5ae2537b5a24ba5b6f703c5.content:
Science doesn't advance in breakthroughs. It advances in replication and nobody films that part.

A result isn't real until a separate lab with separate equipment and separate people gets the same number, which takes years. It's boring, it's unglamorous, and it's the entire foundation.

The people closest to the work are almost always the least confident about grand claims, because they know how many things could have gone wrong. The people furthest from the lab are the most certain, and that inversion tells you where to put your trust.

I read a paper last week. It said conclusive three times. I went looking for the replication and found none. None at all. I filed it under interesting and moved on. That's the whole habit.

That isn't cynicism. It's just the difference between a result and a finding. I'm more optimistic about the slow grind than the flashy headline. The grind is where progress lives, one confirmation at a time.

1e37b12fa09b0e198dbf8d8113acfc30e9ede796.content:
The most useful thing I did this month was write down every time an AI tool surprised me.

Not the big surprises. The small ones. It guessed my variable name right and forgot what we agreed two messages ago. It rewrote something I hadn't asked it to touch.

Two pages later a pattern showed up that I would never have noticed otherwise. It's confident about structure and careless about scope. Great at the shape of a thing. Rubbish at remembering the edges I drew. So I changed how I talk to it. I give the structure question first and then I lock the scope down in a separate message. Fewer surprises, less fixing.

I never saw this written down anywhere. Not one article. I had to trip over it four times before I started keeping notes. The notes took five minutes a day. They are the highest return thing I have done all year, which says something about how little I was paying attention before.

Tools don't change. They keep doing what they do. What changes is whether you can see the shape of it.

Every feature request we get can be traced back to a sentence somebody didn't understand.

Not a missing number. A missing explanation. So we spend a lot of time on plain English, and I mean that as an engineering constraint rather than a tone of voice. If a screen needs a glossary, it's broken.

The test I use is whether my dad would get it. He's not stupid, he just doesn't work in finance, and he's not going to look up "adjusted" before deciding whether he cares. If the answer depends on him knowing one industry word, I've shipped a bad answer.

I'm still surprised by how much harder simple is. Jargon is a shortcut. It assumes you already know. Writing "the company made less per sale than last quarter" takes 4 more drafts than "margin compression".

I have never once looked at a finance tool and wished it were more technical. Not once.

I stopped watching tutorials and started breaking things and my progress tripled.

A tutorial is a promise that nothing will go wrong. That's the wrong promise for someone trying to learn. You finish it, everything works, and you have no idea why. Breaking something is different. You have a real question with a real cost. The answer sticks because you paid for it.

The first time I deleted a file I shouldn't have I spent forty minutes putting it back, and I have never made that mistake again. Forty minutes was the price of the lesson and it was cheap. I still use docs constantly. Docs are reference. Tutorials are theatre.

The shift happened when I started asking what happens if instead of how do I. What happens if I remove this. What happens if I run it twice. What happens if the network drops here.

I have never found a video for those questions, they just have an answer, and you find it by looking. I'm not against learning from other people. I'm against the version where you watch and never touch.

I read a physics paper every week and I understand maybe a third of it. I keep doing it anyway.

The parts I don't understand are the useful part. They give me a shape of what I'm missing. A vocabulary I don't have yet. Questions I can't even form properly.

The parts I do understand are not that surprising. It's the fog that teaches you where your map ends. Nobody tells you that reading above your level is a skill you can practice. It feels bad the whole time. You finish a page and can't summarise it and that feels like failure.

It isn't failure. It's calibration. I write one sentence after each paper about what I think it claimed. Six months of those and I can see which fields I have learned something about, and which I have just visited.

That list was humbling. I thought I was following a lot more than I was. Being confused on purpose, regularly, and writing down what confused you, is the best route I have found from not knowing to knowing.

Star ratings on app stores measure almost nothing and I learned that the expensive way.

I shipped something that I thought was clean. Two reviews appeared on day one. Both said the same thing about a screen I had tested maybe fifty times.

I thought they were wrong. They weren't wrong. They were using it in a way I had never imagined because I built the flow and I already knew where everything was. The blind spot is always your own familiarity. You can't test your way out of it because the test exists in your head.

So now I watch one person use it without saying anything. No instructions. No pointing. Just watching where the cursor goes and where the pause is.

Every single time that has found something. Every time. The feedback isn't the review. The feedback is the pause. I treat the review as a receipt for a mistake I already made three weeks ago and shipped anyway.

A demo of an AI finance tool and the thing you'd trust with your portfolio are about 90 percent different work.

I learned that here. Making a model answer a question is a weekend. Making it answer the same question the same way, with the right source attached, at 8:30 in the morning on a heavy news day, is the job. Demos don't have bad days. Products do.

So I spend my time on the unglamorous half. What happens when a provider is slow. What happens when a filing lands 10 minutes late. What the screen looks like when we have nothing to say, because that's a real answer and it shouldn't look like an error.

I've shipped features that looked great in a demo and I'd rather not do it again. Trust is built in the boring cases.

edc41166b2383d1b2d689508a04bd2a2a05ff195.content:
The most underrated AI skill is knowing when the output is confidently wrong.

This isn't about hallucination in the obvious sense. It's about code that runs, passes a quick look, and does something different from what you asked. No error and no warning, just a semantic drift that shows up in production.

I caught one last week. The function took a list and returned a list. Correct types, correct shape. It dropped duplicates the whole time, which I never asked for and never noticed because my test data had none.

I would take a crash over that. A crash tells you, while a quiet wrong answer compounds. I don't defend against it by reading carefully. I ask what this does that I didn't ask for. Then I look for that on purpose.

Reading for correctness is slow and you stop seeing it after two minutes, while reading for surprises is fast and stays sharp, and nobody trains it. Every guide is about getting output, not about auditing it. The auditing is the job. The rest is typing.

Sleep research is the one area where the findings are boring and unambiguous and we all ignore them anyway.

The evidence doesn't argue. Consistent timing matters more than total hours, and light in the morning and dark at night does measurable work. Caffeine has a half life and it's longer than the afternoon. Nobody acts like it.

None of this is a secret. Every part of it's published, replicated and cheap to act on, and I ignored all of it for years while reading about it, which is the strange part. I had the information and didn't act, which means the information was never the bottleneck.

I tested one thing for 30 days. It was a rule, not a habit. Same wake time every day, including weekends, and everything else followed because the rest of the day has an anchor to sit on.

The research is clear and my behaviour wasn't. Being aware of a good idea isn't the same as doing it. Most of us already know that.

I switched to keyboard only for two weeks and found out how much time I was spending on nothing.

No file tree. No clicking around. Just a terminal, a text file, and whatever the tool could do with commands. The first two days were miserable and slow. I had to look up how to do things I did a hundred times a day with a mouse.

By day five something changed. My hands stopped leaving the home row and I stopped losing my place. The little pauses between actions disappeared because there was nothing in between the actions.

The thing I missed most surprised me. Not the file tree. The scrollbar. I didn't realise how often I used position on screen as a memory aid. It didn't change what I built. It changed how much thinking happened between the building.

I'm not a terminal purist now. I use the mouse plenty. But I know which of my habits were load bearing and which were just comfortable. That's worth two uncomfortable weeks.

Local models are good enough for most of what I do and I spent way too long assuming otherwise.

I had this idea in my head that anything running on my own laptop would be a toy. Something to play with while the real work happened on someone else's servers, and that assumption cost me money for months.

Then I started paying attention to what I ask for. Rename this function and explain this error. Write the boring boilerplate for this file. Fix my indentation. All of that is small.

A small model handles small things and runs with no network, no bill, and no waiting. That's the appeal. It answers before I finish rereading my own sentence. The big remote models still earn their place. I keep them for architecture questions, weird bugs, and anything where the answer needs to hold up. I use them about one request in ten. Not often.

The trick is honest routing. Which means I had to notice what I was doing instead of guessing. I wish I had done that audit a year earlier. Turns out most of my prompts were errands, not thinking.

I measured my own output for a month and found out I was wrong about what made me productive.

I assumed the good days were the long ones. More hours, more shipped. It turns out the long days were mostly spent recovering from context switching. The strongest correlation with a good day was one number. How many uninterrupted blocks over forty minutes I had. Not total time. Blocks.

The other surprise was the afternoon. I had been treating it as a second morning for years. It isn't. It's a different animal and I was feeding it the wrong food.

I don't have a productivity system now. I have one number I try to protect. Everything else is decoration on top of that.

Nuclear keeps coming back up in every serious energy conversation and the reason isn't political.

It's the one large source that produces steady power regardless of weather or time of day, and everything else needs either storage or a backup, both of which cost money and land.

The problem has never been physics. It has been time and cost per project. A reactor takes a decade. The budget will be wrong by the end. That's it. Investors hate both of those things and they're right to.

I don't think the interesting question is whether nuclear is good. It's whether anything can be built at that scale on a predictable schedule. I don't have a strong view and I have stopped pretending to. Every time I read a confident take on this topic, the person has picked a side in advance. A grid plan without a steady source in it assumes storage gets very cheap very fast, and that assumption is doing a lot of work.

That assumption might be right. I want it stated out loud instead of buried.

1f32c50ecc53107626d32279e85f6bf7614e6ad5.content:
I stop trusting a tool the moment it starts guessing at my intent.

I have learned to watch for one specific behaviour. When something can't find what it needs and instead of saying so, it invents a reasonable substitute. It creates a file that doesn't exist. It calls a function with made up arguments. It fills a gap with something plausible.

Plausible is the dangerous word. It means the error can't surface until much later, which means the cost of the mistake lands on me instead of on the tool.

I would much rather have a loud failure. Tell me you couldn't find it. Stop. Let me fix the input.

So I look for tools that prefer stopping over guessing, and I have started writing my own little scripts that way. If a required file is missing, exit with a message. Don't create an empty one. That single habit has saved me more time than any feature. An empty file in the right place looks exactly like success and it's never success.

It had refactored a function into something clever. Three layers. An abstraction I didn't ask for. All of it correct, all of it impossible to read six weeks later when I have forgotten why any of it exists.

So I said do it again, simpler, and I want one function. The second version was fifteen lines. Same job. I understood every line of it.

Saying no is a skill and it took me months to develop it. The instinct is to accept whatever comes back because it works. But working and being understood are two different bars, and just one of them matters when I come back to this file in March.

Two hours of my day came back. Not from magic. From being honest about which half of the work I was adding value to.

I follow the unfamous parts of physics. I suspect that's true for most people who follow it.

Black holes are photogenic. They are also a corner case at extreme scales. What shapes what I can do is much more ordinary. Materials, batteries, semiconductors, heat.

Heat runs everything. Getting rid of it's why your laptop throttles, why data centers drink water, and why a phone gets slow in the sun. Semiconductors are the other one. Every advance in what I can build is downstream of somebody making a smaller thing with fewer defects.

Neither topic has a documentary. Both of them set the ceiling on everything else. I started paying attention to the boring parts of science and my sense of what is realistic got much better. Fusion timelines stopped looking like a countdown and started looking like a materials problem with a schedule I can't guess at.

The famous questions are fun. The ordinary questions decide.

The most valuable thing I've worked on here is a connection that just doesn't break, and I can't show anyone a screenshot of it.

Nobody signs up for reliability. They sign up for the thing it enables and they notice when it's gone. Brokerage connections are the least glamorous surface in this product and the one I think about most, because everything else depends on the holdings being right.

So I look at the failures instead of the features. What happens when a provider revokes access. What happens when a sync lands halfway. What a user sees when their positions are 2 days stale, because showing stale data without saying so is worse than showing nothing.

My game runs at a stable frame rate now. It took me three weeks to find a problem that turned out to be eleven lines.

The bug was mine. Two systems were both writing to the same list every frame, and they disagreed about the order. Sometimes it looked fine. Sometimes a character would slide sideways for a frame and snap back.

I couldn't reproduce it on purpose. Not once. That's the worst kind of problem. So I stopped guessing and started measuring. I logged the list length every frame into a file and let it run for ten minutes while I made coffee. When I came back the answer was sitting there in plain text.

That habit changed how I work. When something is weird and I can't explain it, I don't read the code again. I add a line that prints the thing and I go get water.

I think the reason people get stuck is that they try to think their way out of a problem that needs to be observed. The code doesn't care what you believe about it. It cares what's happening right now.

I spent two days reading about data structures and benchmarked three different approaches, and I argued with myself about which was cleanest, while my answer sat in the middle of the function the whole time.

File access inside a loop is invisible when you test with four rows and painful when you test with forty thousand. My test data was tiny and so my confidence was enormous. The fix took six minutes. Move the file handle outside, read once, pass it in.

I have a rule now that comes straight out of this. Before I optimise anything, I go and count the expensive operations. Not the clever path. The obvious path. Noticing beats theory almost every time.

Game feel is a real engineering discipline and most people treat it as decoration.

You can have correct collision, correct physics and correct animation, and the whole thing still feels dead in your hands and no fun to touch. The difference is response time. How many frames between the input and the visible reaction. Whether the camera leads slightly. Whether the sound lands on the same frame as the impact.

None of that is in the design document. I know what people mean when they say a game feels good. I spent a weekend on nothing but this. No new features. Just moving things a few frames earlier and watching the same level become something I wanted to replay.

My animation setup was correct for the first time and the game felt worse than before. I was confused for about an hour. Now I tune feel before I build content. It's easier to add levels to something that feels right than to fix a feel problem under ten levels of stuff.

Most guides skip this. That's a mistake. It's hard to describe and impossible to screenshot.

I wrote money as a decimal and the totals came out a cent off. That cent cost me an afternoon.

A computer stores a decimal as a binary fraction, and some of those fractions can't be represented exactly. So a tenth isn't quite a tenth. Add it a few thousand times and the error shows up where people notice. I stopped using decimals for money at all. Store the smallest unit as a whole number. Cents, not dollars. Then addition is exact because whole numbers are exact.

It feels like a step backwards. It isn't. It's the difference between an accountant trusting your number and an accountant finding your mistake.

I still think about how invisible it was. My test with four rows passed. My test with four hundred rows passed. The drift only appears when you add up a lot of small things, which is what a real total does.

So now anything that people will count in money gets stored as an integer. Prices, fees, balances, totals. No exceptions and no cleverness. One bug taught me a rule I will keep for the rest of my career.

It said the config file was missing and gave the exact path it looked in. That's it. No stack trace theory, no advice, no apology. I hit it at 11pm, read the line, made the file, and moved on. I didn't have to open the source. I didn't have to remember anything.

Compare that to the errors I got from a library last month. Something went wrong. Check your input. Which input. Which line. No idea.

Bad errors cost the reader time and the writer nothing. Good errors cost the writer two minutes and save everyone else hours. It's one of the most lopsided trades in this job and almost nobody takes it.

So now every failure path I write has to say what failed, where, and what to do. If I can't fill those three in, I don't understand my own error case yet. That test has caught design problems before the code even ran.

daa476fd8b853fb5ffd1dd263277e38f5b1ac8e1.content:
I removed a confirmation dialog and my users stopped asking me about accidental deletes.

The dialog said are you sure. Two buttons. I thought it was protecting people. What it did was add a step to a frequent action and catch almost nothing, because people click through dialogs on reflex. The dialog had become a coin flip with a prompt.

So I replaced it with something better. Delete is instant, and a small bar at the bottom says what was deleted with an undo link that stays for ten seconds. Now the fast path is fast and the mistake is recoverable instead of prevented. That's the trade I had backwards. You can't stop someone making a mistake. You can make the mistake cheap.

I found undo harder to build than a dialog. It means the data isn't gone for a moment, which means more care in the layer below. Ten minutes of work.

Since then I ask one question about every confirmation. Am I preventing a mistake, or am I just making the user ask themselves. I usually find it's the second one.

29007b3257588680fcad6aa3338f13c978945f09.content:
I moved one project from a config file to plain defaults and it got used twice as often.

The old version had eleven settings. Port, log level, paths, retries, formats. All reasonable. All documented. All of it a decision I was handing to somebody who just wanted to run a thing.

Every setting is a question, and questions are a tax on starting. The first run is where you either keep a tool or close it forever. So I picked the values I use and hardcoded them. I cut the eleven settings to two. If you need the others, there's an environment variable and a page explaining it.

Nothing broke. Nothing was lost. The people who wanted to tune it still can. The people who didn't now get a working tool in one command.

The thing I got wrong for years is thinking flexibility is free. It isn't. You pay for every option with attention, and attention is the scarcest thing your user has. Defaults are an opinion. I would rather ship mine and be argued with than ship eleven blank boxes.

df731a7c57960b3ea1803dbc5c21fe796ed0a3a7.content:
The most valuable thing I did after a bad outage was write down what I thought happened before anyone explained it.

I wrote it wrong. I was confident and I was wrong in an interesting direction. I blamed a dependency first. The real cause was a change I had made myself two days earlier.

That written guess is why I learned anything. If I had just read the explanation, I would have nodded and moved on. Having a wrong theory on paper forced the comparison. Now I do that after every failure, small or large. Three lines. What I expected, what happened, what would have caught it.

The last one is the only one that changes anything. It turns a vague resolution to be careful into a specific thing I can add. In this case, one alert on a number I wasn't watching.

Two years of writing those down and I have a list of mistakes I have mostly stopped repeating, which is worth more to me than any course I could have taken. Not because I got wiser. Because I wrote them down while they were fresh and painful. That's the whole method and it costs five minutes.

3091f8547a7a4caa8d3aacdfff858989662d0a68.content:
My code assumed every timestamp was in the same timezone and it worked fine for eight months.

Then a user in a different timezone scheduled something and it fired four hours early. Nobody lost money. It was still wrong.

I had been treating a date as a simple value. It isn't. It's a position on a line that depends on who is looking. Two people in two places can disagree about what today means and both be right.

The fix took twenty minutes. Store everything as a single reference and convert only when showing it to a person. That's the whole rule and it's older than I'm. What annoyed me is that I knew this. I had read it. I still wrote the naive version because my test data happened to sit in one timezone, which meant my tests were measuring nothing.

That's the pattern I keep finding. My tests pass because they share my assumptions. They aren't wrong. They're blind in the same place I'm. The bug was never the timezone. It was the confidence.

I pasted the same eight lines into four places and told myself I would tidy it up later.

Later didn't come. Then I fixed a bug in one of the four copies and shipped it. Three still had the bug. Nobody noticed for a month because three of the four paths were rare. The one I fixed was the common one, which is why my testing looked clean.

That's the thing about copy paste. It's not that the duplication is ugly. It's that you now have to remember every copy exists, and you won't. So I have a rule that's probably too strict. Two copies are fine. The third time I reach for the same lines I stop and pull them out.

The reason two is fine is that the abstraction is often worse than the duplication. I have built the shared helper too soon and ended up with a function that takes six flags and does four jobs. That's not better. That's a different mess.

The hard part is timing it. Not too early and not on the fourth copy. I still get that wrong maybe a third of the time.

My first version of anything is always too clever and I have stopped fighting it.

The pattern is reliable now. I sit down, I plan something sensible, and forty minutes later I have built a small framework. An abstraction. A thing that could handle cases I will never have.

Then I use it for a day and it annoys me. The second version is smaller and the third is almost nothing. The third is the one that survives. What changed isn't my instinct. It's my willingness to skip ahead. I now go straight to writing version three on purpose, which means ignoring the framework idea and writing the direct thing.

It doesn't work every time. Sometimes the clever version was needed, but that happens far less often than my brain insists it will.

The skill isn't having good first instincts. It's recognising your own predictable mistakes in time to route around them. I know what my brain does first. So I do something else first. Same every time.

306c96cde0d8a4071fc2ab6e762915184b41eba1.content:
I added a type annotation to a file and the compiler found three bugs I had shipped a week earlier.

None of them were dramatic. A value that could be missing, passed where it had to exist. A number passed where the function wanted text. The kind of thing that works until the one input that breaks it.

That's what I wanted from types. Not correctness proofs. Just a machine reading my code with fresh eyes and pointing at the places where I was vague. Being vague is the natural state. You write a function and it takes a thing. A thing is fine while you're inside it and confusing the moment you leave.

The annoying part is that I resisted this for a long time. I had decided types were ceremony. What changed my mind was a bug I couldn't reproduce, and a compiler that pointed at it in a second.

I don't annotate everything. I annotate the boundaries. Where data enters, where it leaves, where two systems meet. That's where the vagueness costs the most. Everywhere else I let it be messy and get on with it.

33c3aeb4e0d6f0e2029e1c15084ecfefcb0b3690.content:
I stored a job in memory and lost it when the process restarted, which took me a while to notice because I never restarted it.

The design was simple. A queue in the process, a worker taking items off it. Fine on a laptop that stays on. Not fine anywhere else.

I learned that a process isn't permanent. It crashes, it gets redeployed, the machine reboots. Everything in memory goes with it, silently, and nobody gets an error. So the queue has to live somewhere that outlives the process. A table is enough. Pick a row, mark it as taken, delete it when done.

The bit I missed the first time is what happens if the worker dies halfway. The row stays marked forever and that job never runs again. So the mark needs a timestamp and a rule that reclaims anything older than a few minutes.

That's the whole outbox pattern. Store it first, then work. Anything still only in memory is not queued. It is a hope. I lost maybe four jobs before I noticed. Silent data loss is the worst kind because there's nothing to read.

0c43fe90582ee168f878dad77acb87984328fa63.content:
I only trust tests I have watched fail.

That sounds obvious. It isn't, because the natural workflow is to write the test after the code, run it once, watch it go green, and feel good. Green tells you almost nothing. It might be testing the wrong thing. It might be testing nothing. The way to know a test does its job is to break the code on purpose and check that it screams.

I did this on a small utility last month. Nine tests, all green. I broke each function in turn and four of the tests didn't notice. They were asserting on shapes that couldn't change. Decoration.

After fixing them I broke the code again and all nine caught it. That took an hour. It's the most valuable hour in that whole project.

Since then my rule is blunt. A test I have never seen fail is a comment with extra steps. It's slower at the start. It's the reason I can change things later without that feeling in my chest.

Indie games are where the interesting design decisions live because there's no money to hide behind.

9ad20384c049c82eedd1f801465a8919a402dba1.content:
I read code I wrote a year ago and couldn't follow it. That was more useful than any course.

I remembered building it. I remembered thinking it was clear. What I couldn't remember was why this file had three entry points and a function that returned two different shapes depending on a flag. Past me had reasons. Past me didn't write them down. So present me was reading a decision with the reasoning cut off.

That's what most bad code actually is. Not stupidity. A reasonable choice, made under pressure, with the context lost.

So I changed one habit. When I make a decision that isn't obvious, I write one line explaining it for whoever reads next. Half the time that person is me, and I'm a stranger to my own work by then.

The other thing it did was make me less precious. I stopped defending old code. It was written by somebody with less information and no reason to feel bad about that. Reading my own history is the only review I get with no social cost.

107ab55b39a2c8f5eaf2e6c31e00f6e6e8b8c6ed.content:
Every energy argument I read skips the same step, which is how much of the power we make is wasted.

Everybody argues about generation. Solar versus nuclear versus gas. That argument is loud and it's also not where the biggest number lives.

The grid loses power in transmission and buildings lose heat through walls. Data centers spend a shocking share of their draw on cooling the machines they just heated up, and fixing that waste would shrink the generation debate. That's less exciting than a new reactor, which is why nobody campaigns on it.

I care about this because I build things that run on servers. My own little tools have a footprint and I have never once measured it. That's on me. I should. The uncomfortable part is that efficiency is boring. Insulation doesn't photograph well. Nobody writes a viral post about better ductwork.

But the cheapest kilowatt hour is the one you didn't need. I have never heard a serious person in energy argue otherwise. Almost nobody in the public argument repeats it.

dcfb2decd8caac2c6aa5aaa37787924c0a279714.content:
I put a password in a file and committed it, and that mistake is permanent in a way I didn't understand.

Deleting the line later doesn't help. The history keeps it. Anyone who clones the repo can read every version back to the first one.

I got lucky. It was a test key for a service I didn't care about. I rotated it, deleted the whole repo, and started again. Twenty minutes and no real harm.

What I took from it's that a leaked secret isn't a mistake you fix. It's a mistake you respond to. Rotate first, clean up second. The order matters because the value is compromised the moment it's pushed.

So now the config lives in an environment file that never gets committed, and there's a checked in example file with fake values so a new machine knows what to set. Nothing clever. No vault, no encryption, no ceremony. Just a hard line between what's in the repo and what isn't. It's the least interesting habit I have and the one I'd least want to drop.

I kept a function around for two years because removing it might break something.

It was used exactly nowhere. I checked twice, six months apart, and both times the answer was the same. Nothing called it.

What kept it alive was the possibility. What if some path I haven't thought about needs it. What if a user hit it in a way I can't see. That fear is real when you have users. It's a fantasy when the only user is you and the whole thing runs on one machine.

So I deleted it. Nothing broke. The file got shorter, and the shorter file took me less time to read the next week. Now I use a blunt test. If I can't name who calls it, it goes. If I'm wrong, the error is loud and instant and I put it back in a minute.

The cost of deleting something you needed is tiny. The cost of keeping things you don't is a file that's slow to read forever. I had those two costs backwards for a long time.

I asked a model a question I already knew the answer to, and it told me I was wrong with total confidence.

That's the part that gets me. Not the error. That it was fluent and wrong at the same time, in the exact register of something that had checked. I caught it because I knew the domain. If I hadn't, I would have shipped it.

So I stopped using model output as an answer and started using it as a first draft from somebody who has read everything and verified nothing. I keep the claims I can check. The rest is a useful shape with the substance missing.

The trick that helps most is asking it to argue the other side. A model that has to disagree with itself will show you where the seams in its own answer are, and they are usually in the places you would not have thought to check.

I trust it more now. That means I check it more.

My deploy used to scare me and that fear was quietly making my code worse.

If shipping is frightening, you bundle. You wait until three changes are ready so you pay the fear once. Which means three changes land together, and when it breaks you don't know which one did it.

I was doing that. Then I made the boring change instead. Same day, one small commit, watch it for two minutes.

Turns out the fear was the problem, not the deploy. Once it landed forty times with nothing going wrong, it stopped being an event and became a step. Small deploys are easier to reason about, easier to reverse, and easier to spot. The one thing they're worse at is feeling dramatic. I will take it.

I care about the tooling here but it's not the point. What matters is time from commit to running, measured in minutes. If that number is hours you will batch, no matter how disciplined you think you're. Mine is about ninety seconds now, which is short enough that waiting to bundle three changes together costs me more than shipping them one at a time. That single number changed how I write code more than any technique I have read about.

5e1f071eb6c4bcbc7490e2451ee78719c8f0fe8c.content:
I turned off most of my alerts and started noticing real problems sooner.

I used to get an email about everything. Disk usage, a slow query, a spike in requests. All true, none of it urgent. Within a month I had trained myself to ignore the whole channel, which is worse than having no alerts at all. An alert you don't act on is noise with a badge. It teaches you that warnings are normal, which is the opposite of what an alert is for.

So I cut them down to the ones where I would get up. If nothing bad happens when I ignore it, it isn't an alert. It's a chart, and charts belong on a dashboard I check when curious. That reframe took maybe fifteen minutes and it changed my relationship with the whole thing.

The other half is the opposite problem. A silent failure is just as expensive as a loud pointless one. So for anything that should happen and didn't, there's one check and it fires once.

Two alerts total. Both mean something. I act on both. Fewer and louder beats many and ignored, and I have never once wished I had more of them.

A dashboard I built showed a number going up and to the right for three months and it meant nothing.

Sessions were growing. I felt good about it. Then I looked at where the sessions came from and found one bot hitting the same page on a loop.

f1d0af43239df007a02db1f9a502c9643d1fd47b.content:
I made one endpoint safe to call twice and it changed how confident I felt about the whole system.

It was a create action. Call it once and you get one thing. Call it again with the same request and you got a second copy. A user who tapped twice because the first tap looked slow ended up with two of everything.

I give each request a name. If the server has seen that name before, it returns the original result instead of making a new one. Same request, same answer, every time.

That one change removed a whole class of problem. Retries became safe. A flaky connection stopped being able to duplicate work. My test suite got shorter because I stopped writing tests for the double submission case. It's a few lines and one extra field. What it buys is the ability to retry anything without checking whether it's safe first, and that's worth much more than the code.

I put it on every write endpoint now. Create, update, charge, send. Anything where doing it twice would be a real problem. The boring guarantees are the ones that let you sleep.

I priced my work at what the hours cost me instead of what the result was worth, and I undercharged for two years.

My maths was honest and useless. I counted the hours, added a margin, and sent it. What I left out is that the value to the person paying didn't depend on how long I took. A script that saves them ten hours a week is worth the same whether I wrote it in a day or a month.

So the questions changed. What does this replace. What does a mistake cost them. Would they rather have it next week or in six weeks. Those answers set the number, and the hours only tell me whether I can afford to say yes.

The uncomfortable part is saying a bigger number out loud for the first time. My voice did something strange.

Nobody blinked. I had been the only one anchoring the price.

f9035cbb886d754072abfd32149c3de2fba21f41.content:
My search box returned nothing for a typo and I lost a user in four seconds.

I watched one person type the name wrong. The system compared two strings, found no match, and displayed an empty page with no suggestions. From the user's side the product is broken. They don't know that a character was off.

So I stopped comparing strings for equality and started ranking them by how close they're. I wrote a few lines. No search engine, no index, no infrastructure. Just stop demanding exactness from people who are typing on a phone.

The empty result page got fixed too. It now says what it looked for and offers two things that are almost right. Almost right is a huge amount better than nothing. Nothing tells the user they're wrong. Almost right tells them they're close.

I did it in an afternoon. That is the highest ratio of user relief to engineering effort I have ever shipped, and I have shipped plenty of things that took far longer. I wish I had watched one person use search before building anything else.

AI in game development is being argued at the wrong level and both sides are skipping the interesting part.

I get the argument about art and jobs. It's real. There is a smaller question underneath it and nobody asks it. Which parts of making a game are bottlenecked by human taste and which are just slow?

Animation blending is slow. Dialogue trees are slow. Placeholder geometry is slow. All of that is grunt work and none of it's where the game becomes good.

The design, the feel, the pacing, the moments, that's where taste lives and it isn't on the table. So the honest position is that the grunt work is going away and the taste work is getting more valuable, which sounds encouraging until you remember that the grunt work is where people learned the taste.

You can't skip the boring middle and arrive at judgment, and I don't know a shortcut past it. I've watched it take years for people who are better at this than me. I find that part worrying and it doesn't fit into either side of the argument.

The screen a new user sees before they have any data is the one that decides whether they stay, and I ignored it for months.

My app opened on an empty list. No rows, no explanation, no next step. Just a heading and white space that looked like a loading failure.

I had built the populated version because that's the version I saw every day. My account had data in it. The empty state was a case I never inhabited.

So I made it a real screen. One sentence about what this list will hold, one button that creates the first item, and a small example so the shape is obvious before you commit anything. The drop off on day one moved. Not by much, but it moved, and the change took under two hours.

The lesson isn't about onboarding. It's that I only ever test the state I live in. Every screen has a version with nothing, and that version is the first one most people see. I now check every list and every page with the data removed. It's the cheapest review I know.

I have several phones running Meta's Muse and none of them needed a laptop to set up. The muse-relay that links them together was written by Muse itself. I gave it the problem and it built the plumbing that lets one chat board drive every phone at once.

Muse told me it couldn't run mcp servers. That's wrong. I wrote mcp-gateway instead, and now those phones reach tools and data the chat surface was never meant to expose. It took an afternoon. No team. No permission. No special access.

That is what bothers me. One keyboard driving many phones, each with its own identity and its own accounts, took me days. If I can do that on my own hardware, so can anyone. Meta should treat it as a real hole and close it, because the next person won't be doing it to learn.

1cab369ecec868b80518abed3f019428877fa42f.content:
I built dark mode by inverting my colors and shipped the ugliest version of my own app.

Pure black backgrounds and pure white text. It looked sharp for ten seconds and hurt after ten minutes. The contrast was so high that every paragraph felt like it was shouting. The fix is to stop using the extremes. Almost black backgrounds, slightly off white text, and let the borders do more work than they did in light mode because shadows don't read on dark surfaces.

Then there's the part nobody warns you about. Every hardcoded color in the app doubles. Every green that meant success now needs a version that reads on dark. I had about thirty of them by then and I found them one complaint at a time.

The thing I should have done is put the colors in one place at the start. I didn't. Dark mode is the audit that found out.

It's still worth building. It's just not a filter you apply at the end. It's a promise about how you store color, and you either made it on day one or you're doing a cleanup.

004f07ecc21e26875fad9067f1b292319f0c4a60.content:
I added an animation to my app and it made the whole thing feel slower even though nothing got slower.

A panel slid in over three hundred milliseconds. Pretty on its own. Awful when you open that panel twenty times in a session, because you're now waiting three hundred milliseconds, twenty times, for information you already decided you wanted. Motion has a budget and I had been spending it on the wrong things.

So I cut the panel animation to almost nothing and moved the budget to the places where it communicates something. A row appearing where you dropped it. A button that shows it registered your click. Those tell you what happened. The sliding panel just told you it was important.

I use one rule now. Motion should explain a change of state, not decorate one. The test is simple. If I remove it and nothing is confusing, it was decoration. If removing it makes you lose track of where something went, it was doing a job.

Most of my animations were decoration and I had talked myself into calling them polish.

I wrote the prompt like a specification and the model stopped guessing, which is the whole job.

My early attempts were one line. Fix this. It would fix something, and often it fixed the wrong thing, and I would blame the model for filling a gap I left open. The gap was mine. An ambiguous request gets an ambiguous answer.

So I write three things now. What the input looks like. What the output should look like. What must not change. That last line does most of the work, because most of the damage a model does is to something adjacent that was already fine.

It takes two minutes and it saves the twenty I would have spent reviewing a change I didn't want. I also keep the prompts in the repository next to the code they describe.

A prompt is a decision, and decisions belong somewhere a reader can find them.

I checked my app on a phone for the first time in three months and found four broken screens.

Everything sat above the fold on a laptop. On a phone the same layout pushed the button below the keyboard, cut the heading off mid word, and made one table impossible to read. None of it was hard to fix. All of it had been live for weeks.

The reason is that I develop on a big screen and the narrow case never appears by accident. You have to go looking for it. It's not a bug that finds you.

So I changed my default. When I finish a screen I resize the window down to phone width before I call it done. It's one keystroke.

That single habit caught more problems than the review process I don't have. I also started writing simpler layouts. A layout that survives a narrow screen is usually a tidier one on a wide screen too, because it can't rely on elbow room to hide a bad grouping. Small screens aren't an edge case. They're the default and I was treating them as an extra.

I stopped clicking buttons with my mouse for a week and found three screens I couldn't operate at all.

095b880a91ea166ba729540adec6b82984e50196.content:
A health check that only asks if the process is alive will report success while the app serves nothing.

I built one of those. It returned ok. The web server could answer. The database could be unreachable and it still said ok. So the monitor showed green through an outage that users were writing to me about.

I had the check asking the wrong question. Alive isn't the same as working. So I changed it to do the things a real request does. Read a row, write a row, delete the row. If any of those fail, the answer isn't ok and it should say which one failed.

That last part matters more than the status. A check that says unhealthy sends me looking. A check that says the write failed and the read worked sends me to the answer.

Mine takes about eighty milliseconds now and it has caught two problems before a user did. Cheap insurance.

I found a piece of code I wrote last year and could see it was holding the whole file together and also causing every problem in it.

That's the shape of tech debt and it's not laziness. Somebody made a good decision for the constraints they had. The constraints changed. The decision didn't.

What makes it hard is that the same thing is load bearing and broken. You can't delete it. Things depend on it. You can't leave it because it's where every bug lives.

So the honest move is replacement in place, one caller at a time, with both versions running next to each other until the last one moves. Slow, boring, and it never breaks anything. The version I tried first was a rewrite. I started a fresh file, got three days in, and discovered I had dropped four behaviours that existed in the old code.

That's how I learned to respect the thing. That mess held more information than I could hold in my head. Rewriting is the tempting move and it's usually the expensive one.

War taught a generation of people something the rest of us got from a screen.

That gap isn't going away and I think it explains more political argument than any ideology does. Two people can look at the same event and be describing different things, because one of them has a body memory of it. Technology changed how war is reported and didn't change how it's experienced. I had a feature flag on for eight months and I could no longer remember which way was on.

That's the failure mode nobody mentions. Flags start as a way to test a change without risking the live one. They become a second version of your program, and every combination is a program you have never tested. I had three flags by then, which is eight states. I had tested two.

So I did the cleanup I should have scheduled on day one. The winner became the path. The loser got deleted. The flag got removed from the config.

The whole thing took an afternoon and removed more code than any refactor I had done that quarter. What I do differently now is write the removal date when I add the flag. Not a reminder, a date, in the description next to a link to the task that removes it. Half the value is admitting at creation time that this is temporary.

A flag is a loan against your future attention. It's fine to take. It's not fine to forget you took it.

086130383feeabb8d0d4c4754a0efd85b2ff3d71.content:
A retry loop I added to handle flaky networks nearly took down a service by hammering it.

I thought the logic was careful. If the call fails, wait a bit and try again. Three attempts. What I hadn't thought about is that a failing server is the worst possible moment to send more requests, and everyone retrying at once makes the failure worse.

The fix isn't to retry harder. It's to retry less and agree on a rule. Wait longer each time, so the fourth attempt is minutes later not milliseconds. Add a random offset so a thousand clients don't fire together. That second one is the part I'd never have guessed. Randomness makes the retries spread out instead of arriving in a wave.

Then there's the question underneath all of it. Should this retry at all. If the call isn't safe to repeat, retrying might charge a card twice. Retries need to know that.

Mine didn't. It was one line and it could have duplicated work. I got away with it because the operation happened to be harmless. I got lucky and I've stopped pretending that's the same as being right.

The best thing I did for my FPS was build a tiny level that takes eleven seconds to cross.

No textures. Grey boxes. One room. Just enough to test movement, shooting, and the camera in the smallest space that could still be fun. Every time I changed something about how the player moves I ran that level twenty times in a row. It takes four minutes. I can feel a difference of two frames.

I worked in the real levels for months, which was a mistake. Too much noise. By the time I got to the interesting corner I had forgotten what I was testing. Small test spaces are the game equivalent of a unit test. Not fun to build, not impressive to show anyone, and they catch everything.

I keep three now. Movement. Combat. Camera. Each one fits on a screen.

I care about this because feel is a hundred small decisions and you can't evaluate a hundred things at once in a big level. You need a place where the only thing that changed is the thing you changed.

de93dc710884ced96efdf689b11b2e6964f83735.content:
Two machines disagreed about what time it was by four seconds and it broke a signature check.

The check was correct. Sign with the current time, verify that the time is recent. Simple and standard. My server and the other one had drifted by a few seconds, so a signed request looked like it came from the future.

Nothing was hacked. Two clocks just disagreed, which is normal and expected. The fix is to allow a window. A couple of minutes either side instead of a few seconds. That absorbs normal drift without accepting an old request.

What I learned is that time is a distributed resource and I had been treating it like a local one. I treat every machine as having its own opinion. So now anything involving clocks gets an explicit tolerance, written as a named number in the config, not buried in the code. If it's a security boundary the value matters and someone should have to think about it.

I expected an exotic bug. The cause was ordinary.

79e13677df4198913f59c2849362fa7ddf8cdfdf.content:
Data centers are the new factories and the comparison is more useful than it sounds.

A factory converts inputs into goods and concentrates workers in one place, while a data center converts power into computation and concentrates machines in one place. Both reshape the town they sit in, and both need water, a grid connection, and a fight with the neighbours.

The difference is that a factory was visible. You could see the shift change. You can't see a warehouse of servers doing anything. That invisibility is why the argument keeps missing. People experience AI through an app and never think about the building. The building is the part with the constraints.

Land, power, water, and cooling are the real limits. Not model quality. We are going to hit the physical ceiling long before we run out of ideas. Probably sooner.

I spent a weekend reading about grid queues after a thread like this one and came away less sure, not more. I say this as someone who uses these services daily and has never once looked up where my requests land. That's the honest position. I benefit from infrastructure I don't think about and can't see.

b51a8f659bebf73e947557f5c4d54393bd981026.content:
I tried to load a large file into memory and my program died with no warning and no error message.

No crash dump with a useful line. The process just stopped existing. That's what running out of memory looks like, and it doesn't ask permission. The file wasn't even that big by modern standards. But I was loading all of it, then making a copy, then a third copy while filtering. Three times the size of the file in memory at peak.

So I stopped loading it all. Read it a line at a time, keep a running total, throw each line away when done. Constant memory regardless of file size.

I got the same result in less time and it used almost nothing. Same output, checked against the old version to be sure. That comparison mattered. Turning a whole file operation into a streaming one is easy to get subtly wrong, and the only way I trust it's diffing the output on a real file.

Since then the default is streaming unless there's a reason not to, and the reason has to be written down. Loading everything is the convenient choice and convenience has a ceiling.

2f5e08a375b8aa9222abbd91433a9b21fac40ee6.content:
The most useful thing my manager asks is what happens when this breaks.

Not if. When. The answer gets written down before the feature exists, which sounds like bureaucracy and is the opposite. It's the thing that lets me move fast, because I know exactly where the edges are.

I've worked on teams where the happy path got 90 percent of the attention and the failure got a generic error message. Users don't experience your happy path. They experience the day the provider is slow, and that day decides whether they trust you.

What's cool here is that failure work counts as work. It isn't the tax you pay after the real feature. It's in the plan, it gets reviewed, and nobody has to be talked into it. Failure is a feature here.

I've shipped things that looked great in a demo and I'd rather not do it again. That matters more than a launch date.

I pinned every dependency version exactly and my builds stopped changing under me. That fixed more than I expected.

I used ranges before that, which is the default and feels friendly. You get bug fixes for free. What you also get is a different program on every machine and every day, chosen by someone else, at a moment you didn't pick.

The failure I hit was a patch release that changed a default. No breaking change, no wrong version, just a different default. My code was fine and my behaviour changed. That's the worst kind of dependency problem because nothing announces it. Your code and the library both did what they said.

I keep versions exact now. Updates are a deliberate act on a branch, which I run, which I watch. Boring. A bit more work.

I watched my model bill triple in a week and discovered the problem was what I was sending it, not how much.

Nothing changed about volume. I'd been guessing. What changed is that I had started asking one small model to plan and one large model to type, which is backwards and expensive. The planning is where the thinking is. Cheapening that is how you get a confident plan that is wrong and forty files of work built on it.

So I flipped it. The hard reasoning goes to the expensive model, in a short conversation, with no code attached. Mechanical edits go to the cheap one, in a long conversation, with everything attached.

My bill dropped by more than half and the output got better at the same time. I was surprised and I shouldn't have been.

Where the cost sits is a design decision and I had been making it by accident.

The slowest thing in my app was a database query inside a loop and it was invisible in every test I wrote.

I tested with eleven rows. Eleven queries is nothing. Production had four thousand, which is four thousand round trips, and the page took nine seconds. The code looked tidy. A loop, a lookup, a build. It reads like the natural way to write it and it's the single most common performance mistake there's.

I stopped asking one at a time. Collect every id first, ask once, and match the answers up in memory. One query instead of four thousand. That change took the page to under a second. The code is longer and less pretty. That's the trade and it's not close.

I count the queries in anything that loops now. Not estimate. Count. In development, with realistic data, because eleven rows will never show you this.

The number that matters isn't the query time. It's how many times you ask. Mine was four thousand and I would never have guessed.

I stopped writing tests for the shape of things and started writing tests for the behaviour, and my suite got smaller and better.

Most of my old tests asserted that a function returned an object with four fields. Fine until I add a fifth field and eleven tests fail for no reason. That's a test measuring the wrong thing, and it teaches you to change tests without reading them. Which is the actual damage. Once you're editing tests to make them pass, they stop being a safety net and become a chore.

So the new ones call the thing and check what it did. Given this input, this number comes out. Given that user, this action is refused. Behaviour, stated in plain words.

Those barely ever change, because I don't redesign what the product does. I redesign how it's organised, and the old tests don't care. The other benefit is that they read as documentation. Someone can open the file and learn what the code is supposed to do.

I built a search index for a dataset that a plain filter handled fine forever.

The dataset grew in my head. It was a few thousand rows and I started planning for millions. So I added a database, a sync job, a background worker, and three failure modes I then had to handle.

Two weeks of work. Then I measured. The filter was taking four milliseconds. That's the mistake in one line. I optimised a thing I had never timed, using a scale I had invented, for a future that might not arrive.

I made a copy of my database before a risky change and it saved me from a mistake I had already reviewed twice.

I was renaming a column. Straightforward, checked, and I ran it against a table with two rows of test data. Fine. Then it ran against production, where one column had a constraint I had forgotten existed.

The backup took four minutes to restore. Without it I would have been reconstructing data by hand from logs. Backups aren't interesting and that's exactly why they get skipped. You don't get credit for the disaster that didn't happen.

What I changed afterwards is the part that matters. The near miss became a rule. Before anything that touches stored data I take a copy and I write down the command to undo it. If I can't write the undo, I don't run the change yet.

That last condition is the useful one. Writing the undo forces me to think about what could actually go wrong, which is a different question from whether the change is correct. Twice now the undo line was impossible to write and both times I found a reason not to ship.

I stopped deleting my old version when I rewrote something and started keeping the working one underneath.

The pattern was always the same. New implementation, confident it's better, delete the old one. Then a week later find the one behaviour the old one had that the new one lost. So now the new one runs alongside the old one, both behind a flag, and I compare outputs on real inputs for a few days. When they agree for long enough I delete the old one.

I used to call that delay indecision, and it has caught something every single time. Twice it was a rounding difference. Once it was an empty input the old code treated as fine and the new one as an error.

None of those were in my tests, because my tests were written against my understanding, and my understanding is what I just replaced. The rule underneath is that replacing behaviour is riskier than adding behaviour. My confidence is highest exactly when I should trust it least.

The old version isn't sentiment. It's a witness.

Infinite patience isn't a feature. I learned that from a request that hung forever.

Nothing crashed. It was silent. Nothing logged an error. The request just sat there, and so did the user, and so did a worker thread that I never got back. A timeout is the boring line of code everyone writes last, and its absence turns one slow dependency into a dead process.

I found it by accident, which is the worst way to find anything. Two hours of reading logs that said nothing, then a hunch and a test.

I have a rule now. Every call that crosses a network boundary gets a deadline, and the deadline is short enough to be useful. If the other side is slow, I'd rather know in five seconds than wait forever and learn nothing. I also count how many of those deadlines fire.

That count is the metric I was missing. It told me one service was failing quietly for weeks.

The bill arrives later. One stops getting updates. One changes its licence. One pulls in eleven more packages because it also needed a date library. I have spent more time reading changelogs for code I didn't write than I ever saved by not writing it.

So the test I use is whether I could replace it in a day. If yes, I write the version I need, which is about forty lines and does one thing. If no, I take the dependency and I write down why.

I have removed nine packages this year. Nothing got worse.

I don't know whether that's clever or incoherent. I've read commentary arguing both, including an analysis that said a million units would raise the installed compute in China by a large multiple. That's a real cost and the people writing the policy know it.

So the honest summary is that the security argument lost to the commercial argument, and the tariff is the receipt. Not a reversal. A hedge.

My position is the boring one. If the goal was slowing a competitor, this does the opposite. If the goal was capturing revenue, it works. Those are different goals and only one of them was stated.

A client asked me for a discount and I said yes before I'd done the math. Then I did the math.

The number they wanted was about thirty percent below the hours I'd already logged. I'd agreed to it in a sentence, in a meeting, because saying yes is easy and the silence after no is uncomfortable.

I emailed back the next morning. Two options. Same scope at the original price, or the smaller scope at their number. They picked the smaller scope and we both stayed friendly.

I've used that email maybe forty times since. Two options, no lecture, same friendly tone. Works better than a rate card, and it takes four minutes.
