Reproducibility gets treated as a bureaucratic chore. I think it's the most interesting part of science.

Here's why. A result you can reproduce is a result you can build on. A result you can't is a story, and stories don't stack. Every lab that publishes a method is either saving somebody a year or costing them one, and there's no middle.

I've watched this in software. Code that ships with tests gets used. Code that ships with a promise gets rewritten by the next person, and the rewrite takes longer than the tests ever would have.

So when I read about a discovery I want to know whether anybody else has run it since. Not because I doubt the finding. Because the second run is the evidence that matters for anybody downstream.

That's my position on the whole thing. Replication isn't a formality. It's the product. Everything else is a claim.

The best test suite I've ever seen belonged to a team that did almost no manual testing. They didn't have better engineers. They had a rule about every bug.

One bug, one test, no exceptions. Not a doc, not a ticket. A test that fails before the fix and passes after. I've adopted that and it changed how many bugs come back.

I asked an accountant to explain a balance sheet to me twice and the second time it landed. The trick was the questions I brought.

Somebody asked me whether AI will replace developers. I've been asked this about thirty times in two years and my answer keeps getting shorter.

No. It will replace the part of the job that was never the job. Typing. Boilerplate. Setup. Forty minutes of nothing. What's left is the reading, the deciding, and the owning, and those three are what a developer always was.

A client paid me ninety days late and the only thing that saved me was a sentence I'd written in the contract because a friend insisted.

The sentence said work pauses on unpaid invoices over thirty days. No drama, no lawyer. I sent one message quoting my own line, and the money arrived in two days along with an apology about an internal approval queue.

Two things I changed after that. Milestones instead of one big invoice at the end, and a deposit that covers the first two weeks. Both of those are boring and both of them are the difference between a bad month and a panic.

What I'd tell anybody starting out on their own is that the contract isn't for the bad client. It's for the good client having a bad quarter. Nobody plans to stiff you. They plan a payment run and you're not on it.

I've never enforced the clause twice. Once. That's it. The clause existing does most of the work.

I've stopped asking whether a tool is good and started asking whether the people behind it will answer in three years.

I've become suspicious of AI detection tools and I want to be fair about why.

They guess. A detector that says eighty percent generated is telling you a classifier fired, and classifiers are wrong on a regular basis. I've watched people accused of using a tool they never used, with a percentage as the evidence.

The asymmetry is what bothers me. A false positive lands on a person. A false negative costs nobody. Any tool with that shape will get misused, and the misuse is happening now in schools and in hiring.

I still think the underlying question is legitimate. A person deserves to know whether they're arguing with a machine. I just don't think a probability score is an answer.

What I'd trust is provenance. Metadata attached at creation, verifiable, standard. That's a harder problem and it's the one that doesn't punish honest people. It's also the one nobody is funding.

Preprints are the best and worst thing in science and both parts are the same property. Nobody filtered it.

That's the trade. Speed, access, and no gate. I've read findings on a preprint server a year before a journal saw them, and I've read things on the same server that should never have been posted.

The fix isn't a gate. The fix is a habit, and the habit is to read the methods and check the data before I repeat the claim. I've watched people skip that step because a number looked official.

So I treat a preprint as a lead and nothing more. It's a lead with a person attached and a document attached, and that's more than a headline gives me.

I'd take the open server over the closed one. Every time. I'd just never confuse a lead with a finding, and the confusion is the whole risk.

I keep a file of predictions with a date next to each one, and the file has taught me more than any book about myself.

Forty one entries now, going back three years. About half came true. The interesting part isn't the score. It's which half. Every prediction I made about other people and money was right, and every prediction about timelines was wrong in the same direction.

I've been asked five times this year how to pick what to write about. My answer is a filter with three questions and the first one does most of the work.

Could I defend this in a comment thread. Did something happen to me that produced it. Would I say it out loud to somebody I respect. Three yes answers and I write it. Three is the bar.

Procurement cycles decide what gets fielded and they run on a clock nobody in the technology world respects. I've watched a good system lose to a worse one because the worse one fit a contract.

That's the part that surprises engineers. The best tool doesn't win. The tool that matches an existing line item wins, because the budget already exists and the process already anticipates it.

I've watched this in government and in large companies. The purchasing path is the product. A team that understands the path beats a team with better technology, and it beats them every time.

So when I see a smart young company announce a defence contract I check whether they hired a procurement person first. If they did, they'll be around in five years.

That's not cynical. It's the cheapest prediction I can make and it's been right more often than wrong. By a lot.

I broke a build on a Friday with a whitespace change. Not a clever mistake. A pointless one.

The diff was one line. A formatter I'd run out of habit reformatted a template and the parser on the other side didn't like it. Took forty minutes to find, because nobody reads a one line change carefully.

Junior hiring fell 8% in six quarters at the companies that adopted AI, according to PwC. Eight percent sounds small. It isn't.

A junior hire isn't there to produce output. A junior hire is the training pipeline. It's how an industry turns a graduate into somebody who can run a project in eight years. Cut the pipeline and nothing breaks this year. Nothing breaks next year either.

It breaks in 2034, when there's nobody in the middle and every team needs a senior at once. I don't think these companies decided to break it. I think each one made a locally sensible call about a cost center, and a thousand sensible calls added up to an industry with no entry level.

Slow internet for two years made me a better developer and I didn't notice until it got fast.

I tracked every hour for one week and hated the answer. Forty one percent of my time went to things I couldn't name.

I dropped a tool I'd used for four years and the reason wasn't the price. It was the export.

Everything I'd built lived inside it in a format only it understood. When I asked how to get my own data out, the answer was a support ticket and a promise. That's when I understood I didn't own the thing I'd built.

So I moved. It took six weeks and the first three were the worst kind of work, because nothing looked better at any point. Then it was over and I could read my own data in a text editor.

I write short sentences now and it isn't a style choice. It's because long ones let me hide.

When I'm unsure, my sentences get longer. I add clauses, I qualify, I hedge. The hedge feels careful and it's actually a way to avoid saying anything that could be checked.

I caught myself doing it in a design document. Read the paragraph out loud and couldn't tell what I was recommending. Four sentences. Nine hedges. Zero decisions.

So I cut. Now the rule is that the recommendation goes in the first sentence of the section and it's one clause long. Everything after that can be as long as it needs to be, because it's supporting a claim instead of avoiding one.

I see the same thing in posts, in emails, in code comments. Short sentence, then the reasoning. Nine years of writing and I've never once regretted the short one. Not once.

So when I write about space I try to write about the pipeline. Instruments, calibration, the people who check the calibration. That layer is where the result comes from and it's the layer nobody claps for.

A new telescope result isn't a fact. It's an argument with error bars attached, and the error bars are where I start reading.

I've done this long enough to have habits. I look for the sample size. I look for whether the effect is marginal or large. I look for a second instrument backing the first one. Most of the time the answer to all three is thin.

That'sn't a criticism of the scientists. It's how knowledge works. A marginal result from one instrument is a lead, not a discovery, and the paper usually says so in language the press release drops.

The press release is the problem. Nobody writes the headline in the paper. Somebody in a communications office writes it, and the communications office has a different job than the researcher.

So my advice is boring. Read the paper. Read the numbers. If you can't read the paper, read the methods section anyway, because the methods section is where the caveats live. I'll keep doing that and I'll keep saying when I get it wrong.

d3d064deab7ce6d9549806d4b57c47c9d3f7160d.content:
Google reported an error correction result in February where adding more qubits lowered the error rate instead of raising it. That threshold is the whole ballgame in quantum.

I'll explain it in one paragraph because most coverage skips it. A quantum machine is noisy. You fix noise with redundancy, so you need many physical qubits per logical one. If the extra qubits bring more noise than protection, the machine can never scale. Crossing that line means scaling becomes a design problem rather than a wall. That's the line.

I read that as a physics milestone and not a product. The gap between a logical qubit that beats the threshold and a machine that factors a useful number is enormous, and it's filled with engineering.

I've watched quantum coverage for a decade and it swings between fifteen years away and next Tuesday. Both are wrong. Every time. The honest version is that the physics got a lot better this year and the schedule didn't.

So I'd keep watching the coherence numbers and ignore the stock moves. The numbers are real. The moves are a mood.

Quantum error correction crossed a threshold this year and I want to be careful about what that doesn't mean.

It doesn't mean encryption is broken. Nothing close. It doesn't mean a useful machine ships in 2027. It means the scaling argument changed from impossible to expensive, and expensive is a category engineers know how to attack.

I've read three results in this space now and they share a shape. A modest number of logical qubits, a small improvement per qubit added, and a paper that's honest about the gap to anything commercial.

The gap is the story. Filling it requires fabrication, cryogenics and control electronics at a scale nobody has built. Each of those is a decade of its own if it goes wrong.

I keep writing this because the hype cycle keeps running ahead of the papers. The papers are good. That's all they are. They aren't a product, and the difference matters to anyone deciding where to spend the next five years.

aba42b39c4bb61fd15a4edcf1f006bd89536f130.content:
A weather model from August beat the public alternatives on storm track by more than thirty hours of accurate lead time. I read that number three times.

Thirty hours isn't a small improvement in forecasting. It's the difference between a voluntary evacuation and a mandatory one. It's fuel staged in the right county. It's a hospital moving generators before the water arrives.

I've watched the machine learning weather models since the first ones landed and the pattern is consistent. They are cheaper, they run in minutes, and they're better at some variables. Physics models still win on others.

The interesting part isn't which wins. It's that a slower, more expensive model and a fast one disagree, and a forecaster has to decide which to trust on a Tuesday night. That's a human problem sitting on top of a compute problem.

I don't think this needs hype. It needs a verification loop, because a model that's right about tracks and wrong about intensity will still get somebody killed.

The scary version of autonomous weapons isn't a robot deciding to kill everyone. It's a system that works as designed and someone dies anyway.

I believe that more than any of the loud versions. A boring failure is easier to ship, because nobody in the chain sees a red flag. A model reports a target with confidence and everybody downstream reads the number as permission.

That's how a normalised bad outcome happens. Not one decision. A thousand small ones, each defensible on its own, each made by somebody who never sees the person at the other end.

I've written about this before and I'll keep writing about it. The danger isn't the hardware. The bug only happened on the customer's machine and I spent two days refusing to believe it. That refusal cost more than the bug.

I asked for logs, screenshots, a video. I reproduced it in four different browsers. Then I finally asked the one question I'd been avoiding. What are you doing right before it breaks. The answer was two words and it was a workflow I'd never imagined.

He was pasting from a spreadsheet with a column of phone numbers formatted with spaces. My validation handled everything except a space, and the error it threw pointed at a different line, which is why four browsers agreed with me.

The National Weather Service estimated that the AI version of its global model uses a fraction of a percent of the compute its physics version needs. Point three percent is the figure I saw. Reduce it by that much and you change who can run a forecast.

I think that's the part that goes underreported. Not accuracy. Access. A model that costs a hundred times less can run at a regional agency, a university, a country that couldn't afford the machine before.

I've watched this happen with mapping and with language models. The cost curve drops and the users multiply. The capability stops being a monopoly of the organizations with the biggest clusters.

I know what else it means. The failure modes multiply, because the cheap model gets trusted by people who can't check it. That's the trade and it's the same trade in every domain where a tool gets cheap.

So I read this as positive with a caveat. Cheap forecasts save lives. Cheap forecasts that nobody validates create a new kind of blind spot. Both are true at once.

The logs told me the request was fine and the logs were wrong, because I'd written the log line. That's a specific kind of blindness worth a paragraph.

My middleware logged after the handler resolved, which meant every failure looked like a success with a slow response. I'd been reading that column for months and using it to argue that the errors were elsewhere.

What broke the loop was a stranger reading my log format out loud. He asked what the field meant and I said it meant the request completed. Then I heard what I'd said.

I've applied that test to every dashboard since. What does this number measure, in the order the machine does things. If I can't walk the path in my head, the number is decoration.

Working remote for four years cost me something I only noticed after I went back in. The small arguments.

Ten years in and I still can't do one thing well. I can't write a simple regular expression without testing it four times, and I've stopped pretending otherwise.

I've watched people who are genuinely good at this, and they're good in a way I can't copy. They see the pattern in their head. I see it after the fourth failure, which means my version costs four test runs and takes twenty minutes.

What changed was the shame. For years I'd hand write something complex to look competent and then debug it for an hour. Now I write the dumb plain version. Three string checks in a row. Then I move on.

That's a trade I'd defend. Two minutes of unglamorous code versus forty minutes of fiddling, and the dumb version is easier for the next person to read, which matters more than my pride.

I keep a list of the things I'm bad at. It's short and specific and it saves me from starting problems I'll lose to. Knowing where you're weak is the cheapest shortcut there is.

76bce02cd117578a0b25582704c23c862bd92692.content:
Every autonomous weapons debate ends the same way. Someone says the technology is coming and can't be stopped. I've started asking a different question.

Which decision is a human still making, and is it on the record. That's it. A targeting system that suggests and a human who approves is a different machine from one that approves itself, and the difference isn't the model. It's the paperwork.

I don't think the treaty track produces a result. Plenty of countries have real programmes and none of them wants to go first. So the practical lever isn't a ban. It's a rule about records, written into the procurement contract.

That's the boring version. Every contract can carry one line about what gets logged and who signs it. I'd take a boring rule over a noble statement, because the contract gets enforced and the statement gets filed. A contract is the only document both sides have to live with.

8e6efc5bca4c8550fb7b4136d681ccb4ba10c735.content:
Before I trust any dashboard I check one number by hand. It's the slowest habit I have and it's the only one that has never failed me.

Last time I checked a conversion figure against the raw table, the dashboard was about nine percent high because a filter counted a retry as a new user. Nobody had lied. Somebody had defined user in a way that made the graph nicer.

I've found four problems that way in three years. Two were definition issues, one was a timezone, one was a job that ran twice on Sundays. None of them would ever have surfaced from inside the tool.

I do it on a Monday. Ten minutes. I pick one figure, write the query myself, compare. If they match, I trust the rest of the page for the week.

That's the whole practice. Not distrust of the team. Awareness that every metric is a sentence somebody wrote, and sentences have edges.

06219b8e4d7658f51abfe00624cc97785bc2f8f4.content:
A quantum processor from last year posted a result that ran thousands of times faster than the best classical method on one specific problem. Thirteen thousand times is the figure. I don't think the general public read it that way. They read it as a finish line.

It'sn't one. It's a demonstration on a task that was chosen, in part, because the hardware could win at it. That's legitimate work and it isn't the same as a machine that beats a supercomputer at something somebody needs.

I've been reading quantum results for a decade and the honest pattern is that each one narrows the space of what is impossible without closing the gap to what is useful. Both are progress. Only one makes a good headline.

So I hold the same position as with fusion and with humanoids. Watch the boring layer. Error rates, cooling, wiring, control electronics. That layer decides the decade.

The physics is real. The schedule isn't, and the schedule is what everybody quotes.

71c002f9de2e944ee0dc28e54d819b23f99b4e63.content:
Shipping to a real deadline taught me more about scope than any course, and the lesson was unkind. The deadline doesn't move, so the product does.

We had eleven weeks and a list of about thirty features. By week four we had seven working and a list of twenty three. So we did the one thing that works. We decided what the smallest honest version was. Then we built that.

What surprised me was how much of the list vanished without anybody missing it. Nine of those features never came up again in a single conversation, not in the demo, not in the feedback, not in the next planning session.

So the deadline wasn't the enemy of quality. It was the one thing forcing a decision the room couldn't make on its own. Comfortable timelines produce big lists. Tight ones produce a product.

I've tried to keep the discipline without the deadline and it doesn't work. Comfort is stronger than discipline. So I book the demo before I book the work.

a6c8ad0c4c619c6e2941e728f31fac69abe4569f.content:
Raising a concern out loud in a meeting changed its fate, and raising the same concern in a message did nothing twice. I've now watched this three times.

The pattern is brutal. A written concern goes into a thread and becomes a task, and tasks get prioritised, and the priority lands below the thing it's about. Said in a room with four people, the same concern moves the decision.

I don't think it's about writing versus speech. I think it's about who's in the room when the decision gets made, and a message doesn't put you next to the person deciding.

So my rule is a threshold. If the concern would cost a day, I write it down and I also say it out loud at the next meeting where the decision is on the table. Writing is the record. Saying it is the lever.

I've watched two people learn this the hard way this year. Both were right. Neither was in the room.

1d3b6509854a36893a36623a80775e3ad690b3bb.content:
My worst mistake at work was a config change at four on a Friday and I'd been proud of how small the diff was.

One line. A connection pool size I'd doubled to fix something during the week. It worked all afternoon and it took the database down at about eight in the evening, and the person who got the call was somebody I'd never met.

The technical cause was simple. I'd raised the limit without raising anything else on the path, so the pool ate the connections the background jobs needed. The lesson wasn't technical at all. I'd made a change that looked small and had no test that could fail.

Since then any config change gets a number next to it. What it is now, what I'm changing it to, and what I expect to see if it's wrong. Three lines in a message to somebody else, every time.

Nobody reviews my configs. That's exactly why the message exists, because writing the expectation down is the only review available at four on a Friday.

9b7134a386c8e939ec74ffa7d2410f220be3e3d8.content:
I hired somebody whose resume didn't match the role and it was the best call I've made in a decade. His last three years had nothing to do with what I needed.

What got him the interview was a paragraph at the bottom of his application about a system he'd rebuilt for a small charity. No scale, no stack buzzwords. He explained the constraint, what he tried first, and what he'd do differently.

I asked him one question in the interview. What's the hardest thing you've had to change your mind about. He talked for four minutes about a caching decision he'd defended for a month and been wrong about.

Six weeks. One finding. He found a flaw in our data model that the team had been building around for a year. Nobody hired him for that. Somebody hired him for the paragraph and the four minutes.

I look for the change of mind question in every interview now. Resumes describe what somebody did. That question describes what they're like when they're wrong.

c742b6d3b9c16d0eef716ed5ae77936a351de159.content:
My first conference talk was nineteen minutes long and I spent eleven of them reading my own slides. I know the numbers because I watched the recording twice.

Nobody told me it was bad. That's the cruelty of a polite audience. They clapped, three people said nice talk, and one person asked a question about a footnote, which I now believe was pity.

What fixed it wasn't practice. It was cutting. The second version had eleven slides instead of thirty four and four stories instead of a feature tour. Same talk, four minutes shorter, and people remembered the stories.

So my rule for any talk is one slide per point and the point has to survive without the slide. If the slide is doing the work, I haven't done the work.

I've given about a dozen talks since. None of them were great. All of them were better than the first one, and that's the only comparison worth making.

9385583c885d10cd4b31ec23ef397b2dee955c75.content:
A bipartisan bill from September would have the National Security Agency write a security plan for advanced models. That's the shape of what's passing instead of a safety law.

I find that telling. The one area with movement is the one framed as national security, because that's the frame that gets a vote. Safety language dies. Security language moves.

I don't think the distinction is fake. A model that can find software vulnerabilities is a genuine security question. But the same capability is the thing people are worried about, and the only version that gets funded is the one about somebody else's country.

So we get capability rules written by the agency that wants the capability, which is exactly the structure I'd worry about if I cared about oversight.

I'd take the bill. I'd also notice what it isn't. One clause inside fifty pages of definitions. It still counts for something.

7e6bb1c59e4b163a1ee3d08f0d5e82c4cc646b91.content:
A teammate quit and the thing he said on his way out stuck with me for a year. He said he'd stopped being able to tell whether his work was good.

I asked one follow up question and got the whole complaint. Seven months. That's how long the signal had been gone. He'd shipped a lot, but the feedback loop had gone soft. Features landed in a dashboard nobody read, the review comments were all style, and no user ever wrote in about his part of the product.

So the work had no signal. Not bad feedback. No feedback. That's the condition that turns a decent engineer into a quiet one, and it isn't fixed with praise.

I changed one thing after that, and it was small. Every project gets a line in the plan about how we'll know it worked, and it can't be a ship date. A number, an email, a support ticket, something with a person attached.

Half of mine still don't get answered. The half that do keep me honest. I'd rather have a soft signal than silence with a badge.

34d92caa470aacd132c1df52f27931f96f15ac8b.content:
I've stopped reading engagement advice and started reading my own comments. The comments are a better curriculum.

Here's why. Advice describes a general audience. My comments describe an actual one. When six people ask the same follow up question, I have a post, and I know it will land because the demand came before the supply.

I've done this for a year. Roughly one in four of my posts started as a question in a comment thread. Those posts do better than the ones I invent, and the reason isn't mysterious.

Most content advice is written for a person who hasn't written anything yet. If you've published a hundred posts, your own data beats every thread about hooks.

So I'd say this. Read your replies before you read a growth guide. Your readers have already told you what they want and they told you for free. That's the cheapest research there is.

f7c1be404abe7164c11436f83e2c6f72f02a860e.content:
I have a file I'm still nervous to open. Nine hundred lines, written by me, four years ago, and it works. That's the problem.

It works and I don't know why, because it's a pile of things that happen to hold together. I've added to it six times without touching the middle, which tells you everything about my confidence in it.

Last month I read the whole thing on a Sunday and wrote a page of notes. Two of the scariest parts turned out to be copies of each other with different names. So I merged them and added a test around the behaviour, and the file lost ninety lines.

That's the strategy for code you're scared of. Don't rewrite it. Read it, name the parts you don't understand, and build a net around each one before you move it. Slow and unglamorous, and it beats a rewrite that fails quietly in a way nobody can debug.

Three parts left on my list. I'll get to them.

3fec3ba01ba7bf3f3d9cf4b217700c8112521c11.content:
I've written two hundred words a day for about fourteen months and the number I care about isn't the word count. It's how long it takes me to start.

It used to take an hour to begin. I'd open a document, rearrange a sentence, close it. The writing wasn't the hard part. The deciding was. Two hundred words is small enough to stop being a decision. It's about fifteen minutes and it fits before anything else, so it doesn't compete with the day.

What changed in the output is the interesting part. I stopped trying to make each piece good and started letting the bad ones exist. About one in eight turns into something worth keeping. The other seven cost me fifteen minutes each.

The internet will tell you this is about discipline. It's about volume and permission. You can't edit a blank page and you can't find the good piece without the bad pieces around it. Lower the bar until starting isn't a decision. Then raise nothing.

f37838a911d68a4b480d82ea205afc698bc1b995.content:
I copied an answer from a forum for eight years before I noticed how often I was wrong about why it worked. Then I changed one habit.

The habit is to read the whole answer, including the votes on the comments objecting to it. That last part is where the real information lives. Twice now the top answer has been the wrong one, and the correction sits three replies down with a fraction of the votes.

What I do with it now is simpler. I read the answer, then I write the reason down in a comment next to the code. If I can't write the reason, I don't paste the fix, because a fix I can't explain is a fix I'll be scared of in six months.

Ninety seconds. That's the cost. It has saved me from shipping at least three things that would have failed on someone else's input.

Search engines gave me access to other people's answers. The job is still mine.

5db40f23c4b7ae5222bace6d726070f7c48b7307.content:
A recruiter called me in July about a role I didn't want and we ended up talking for forty minutes anyway. I learned more from that call than from the three I wanted.

I asked what her clients ask for when they list a position. Half the time the list is what the last person had, not what the work needs. She said she can tell within two questions whether a hiring manager actually knows the job they're filling.

That matched something I'd felt for years and never had a way to say. A role description is often a memory of the person who left. Responsibilities get copied forward because nobody wants to explain why they changed.

She also said the salary band is set before the interviews start and it almost never moves. So the answer to more money is rarely better performance in the process. I took two things from it. Two questions. Ask what the last person did that nobody wants to lose. Ask who set the band and when. Forty minutes. One call.

440958edaf16aa3379b637d1c71b06c89ce68f7e.content:
A default value caused a bug that took five years to find and about forty minutes to fix. I think about the ratio more than the bug.

The default was a timezone. Everything assumed the same one because the first version ran for one customer in one place. When the second customer arrived, nothing broke on the day. It broke on the last Sunday in March, and it broke in a report nobody reconciled until the year end.

The fix was a flag. The lesson was that every default is a decision about who you're building for, and defaults are the decisions nobody reviews because they look like settings rather than choices.

So now I write defaults down. Not in a doc. In a comment next to the line, with the sentence this assumes one timezone. Six months later that sentence is the only reason anybody remembers the constraint.

I've been the person who added the bad default. I'd like to be the person who labels the next one.

5540bd46bb9e91418cca55c3157e6e1a7eec94dc.content:
Customer service is the first job most companies hand to a model and the first one that breaks in public. I've sat in the queue and I've read the transcripts.

Here's the failure I keep seeing. A model handles ninety percent of the volume, the ten percent that needs a human gets stuck in a system designed for the ninety, and the customer has no path out. So a tool that fixed the average case made the worst case worse.

That's a design choice. Not a limit. I've watched teams ship without an escape hatch because the metrics measured containment and containment was the goal.

I don't have a moral objection to automating support. I have a design objection to a system with no door. Every flow I've built has an exit at the top and it costs nothing to add.

So my rule is simple. Automate the tier, keep the human, and make the jump between them one click. One click. That's it. I've never seen that fail a review and I've seen the alternative fail loudly.

c78d48df06362a9f8a9eca0137d19a3575952ba1.content:
The fastest debugging trick I know is deleting things. Not random deletions. Deleting the thing I'm sure isn't the problem.

I built a page that took nine seconds to load and I spent two days on the network tab. Then I removed an analytics script that I knew couldn't matter, and the page loaded in one second. It mattered.

I think the reason it works is this. Being sure is the symptom. When I'm certain something is innocent, I've stopped looking at it, and the bug is hiding in the category I've excluded from the search.

So now I delete in halves. Take out the top half of a suspect area, see if the problem survives. Nine seconds becomes four. Then two. Then one. You can find anything in about six deletions if the thing is divisible.

I use the same trick on config files and on CSS. Cheaper than reading, and it doesn't require me to be smart about anything.

4315e36e4b007421faec2a672411132399d3b707.content:
A study with a small sample can still be worth reading. A study with a small sample presented as a large one is not.

I've read enough papers to have a habit and the habit is cheap. I find the number of participants before I read the conclusion, because the conclusion is written to sound complete and the sample size tells you how complete it can be.

There's a case I keep in mind. A sensitivity figure from a handful of patients got repeated in coverage as a general claim about a test. The paper didn't say that. The coverage did, and the coverage was built from the abstract. Nobody lied. Somebody compressed, and compression is how errors travel.

That's the failure mode I care about. Not fraud. Compression. A finding travels one step and loses its error bars on the way.

So my rule is to read the methods section before I repeat anything. It takes twenty minutes and it has stopped me from posting something wrong at least a dozen times this year.

2ccdf750e45d5d4ba196c6180fe22f51c7176076.content:
I fixed a bug yesterday in about four minutes and the reason it was four minutes is that I read the error message before I touched anything.

That's the whole habit. Read the message. Read the line number. Read the second paragraph of the message, which is where the useful sentence sits. Then look at the code.

The older me would open the file and start changing things. That approach feels productive and it costs an hour, because the edits hide the original state and now there are two problems instead of one.

I timed it once out of curiosity. Reading first took two minutes and the fix took ninety seconds. Editing first took about forty minutes on the same class of bug.

There's no cleverness in any of this. The message is the fastest document in the whole system and it's written by the party that knows where the failure happened.

e39d76f710bdf94c04777924b3301ea8ac49c534.content:
I asked four people for feedback on the same piece of work and got three useful answers and one that cost me a week. The bad one came from the most senior person.

He said it needed to be more strategic. That's a sentence that sounds like feedback and contains nothing you can act on. I spent five days trying to guess what he meant before I went back and asked him for one example.

He gave me one in about thirty seconds. He wanted a sentence near the top about who pays for the thing. That was the whole note. Five days of guessing for a thirty second answer.

I have one rule now. If I get a piece of feedback and I can't say what I'd change, I ask for an example before I do anything. Not a clarification. An example. Vague feedback gets specific when you ask somebody to point at a line.

The bad advice wasn't malicious. It was shorthand from somebody who had already done the thinking and forgot to hand it over.

9d6eb8c2de19296ba1790f40e7021ff6878aa85a.content:
I turned a hobby into freelance work once and it took about a year to get the hobby back. Worth writing down because everybody sells that move.

The first three paying jobs were fine. The next five were the same job with different names. Five jobs. One job. By the end of them I'd stopped opening the editor for fun. The thing I used to do to rest had become the thing I charged for, and the rest was gone.

What fixed it was a rule I'd never have written at the start. I don't take paid work in the hobby version of the thing unless the problem is one I'd have chosen anyway. So about one in six inquiries. My weekends belong to me.

I've watched two friends do the opposite and both of them quit the craft. Not out of failure. They got good at it and stopped enjoying it, which is a worse ending.

If you can make money from the thing you love, do it once carefully and keep a piece that nobody pays for.

3e2c6dbf9f4410a45e156167f9a7d84a4770e285.content:
A junior on my team asked the question nobody wanted to hear and saved the quarter. It took her eleven seconds to ask and it cost her something to say.

We were an hour into a planning meeting and everything was agreed. Our plan had four phases and a date. She asked what happens if phase two takes twice as long as we think.

Nobody had an answer. Silence. Everyone had been treating phase two as a duration rather than a risk. Two of the people in the room knew the real number and neither had said it. We rebuilt the plan around the worst case and shipped a version of the thing four weeks earlier. Not the whole thing. The part that's useful on its own.

She told me afterwards she almost didn't ask, because she was new and the room was senior. It was senior. That's exactly why it needed her. Most useful question in a planning meeting is about the assumption nobody has priced.

23a88b5104a882a34df03d74c8edff3f938792e5.content:
I read the terms on a tool I was about to build on and found a clause about using customer data to improve the service. Six lines. Took four minutes.

I asked support one question. Can I turn that off. The answer was yes, in a setting three menus deep that isn't on by default when you sign up through the team plan.

Two things followed. I turned it off, and I now read that section on every platform I put real work into. It's the section nobody reads, which is why it's where the interesting sentences live.

The bigger thing is what it changed about my own product. I added a plain sentence at the top of our own terms that says what we do and don't do with a customer's data, in words a person can read without a lawyer.

Four minutes and one question. That's the whole cost of knowing what you signed.

a19ea6c4dde14901b06815e3e87e42f8269c9644.content:
Everybody wants to talk about the reactor design and nobody wants to talk about the queue. I've spent time in the queue and it's where projects die.

Here's the shape of it. A grid operator has a list of projects waiting for permission to connect. The list is longer than the grid can absorb in a decade. Most of those projects will never be built, and they still hold their place in line.

That's the bottleneck. Not physics. Not funding. A spreadsheet with a waiting list on it, and the waiting list is measured in years.

I don't think people grasp how much this decides. The cheapest generation in the world is useless if you can't connect it, and connection is a process rather than a purchase.

So I'd reform the queue before I'd subsidize another design. I've watched the same pattern in housing and in broadband. The permit is the product.

If I could send one message to myself at twenty two it would be a sentence about saving, and it isn't the sentence I expected to write.

It's this. Put ten percent of every payment somewhere boring before you spend a penny of it. Not for a house. For the day you say no to a client and need to eat for six weeks.

I learned it backwards. My first three years of freelance work went out as fast as it came in, and the first time I turned down a bad project I had about four hundred dollars of buffer and I took the project back three days later.

The math isn't the point. The point is what the buffer does to your behaviour. With six weeks of expenses in the bank I say the honest sentence in meetings. Without it I agree to things.

I've watched a dozen people hit this and the people with the buffer are the people who still like the work. Ten percent. Boring account. Nobody else sees it.

I got an offer last year that was about twelve percent below what I expected and I asked one question instead of arguing. That question was about the range.

The lesson is that a number you don't like is often a category problem. Ask about the band. Ask about the level. Leave the feelings out of the first two messages.

A review of my code came back harsh and I almost answered it with an argument. I'm glad I waited a day.

The reviewer had written eleven comments. Four of them were about taste. The other seven were a list of places where my error handling lied to a user, and one of those would have cost somebody money.

Open weight models keep landing and September was another month of it. The interesting thing isn't the benchmarks. It's who can now run a capable model on hardware they own.

I run local weight models when the task allows. Not because they're better. Because the data stays on the machine and the cost doesn't scale with usage, and for a lot of work those two properties matter more than a leaderboard point.

The trade is real and I want to name it. A local model you can inspect is a local model you maintain. Quantization, context limits, version drift, all of it lands on you. Nobody writes that part in the announcement post.

So my position on open weights is consistent with everything else I write. Boring infrastructure beats a demo. The capability is only useful if you own the failure modes, and owning the failure modes is work.

I'll keep running both. Cloud for the hard problems, local for the private ones, and I check the license before I ship anything.

What changed it was writing down what I was saying no to when I said yes. Not the time. The other task. Saying yes to the small thing is saying no to the thing behind it, and that list got uncomfortable fast.

Yes is cheap in the moment. The bill arrives as a month of work that's fine and none of it is good.

A refactor paid for itself in nine days and I know the number because I counted the support tickets before and after.

A pile of frontier models launched in ten days this month. Five announcements, each with a benchmark table, each claiming a state of the art.

I read the tables and then I go do the thing. That's the only test I trust. A model that wins on a reasoning benchmark can still fail on the specific task I have, and the specific task is all I care about.

I've been through four of these launch cycles now. The pattern is stable. Capability goes up. Price per token goes down. Reliability at the edges moves much more slowly than the middle of the distribution.

That last point is the one that matters for shipping. A model that's right ninety five percent of the time and wrong in a different way each time is harder to build on than one that's right eighty percent of the time in the same way, because you can code around a known failure.

So I don't upgrade on release day. I upgrade when a task I already fail becomes a task I pass.

A copy paste cost me half a day last week and I've stopped treating that as a beginner mistake. I do it too, and I do it when I'm confident.

What happened is boring. I copied a block from a sibling function, changed the three obvious values, and missed the fourth because it sat on a line that looked like commentary. It wasn't commentary. It was the one variable that mattered.

The reason is that copying carries context into a place that doesn't have it. The block was correct next to its neighbour and wrong eight hundred lines away, and reading it back didn't help, because I read what I expected to see.

So now the last step of a copy is a read of the whole thing as a stranger, out loud, with the variables named. Two minutes. It has caught the missing value three times since, which is a better rate than my attention span.

I've stopped calling it laziness. It's a known failure mode of being fast, and the fix is a step rather than a resolution.

Launch cadence went up and the interesting effect isn't the rockets. It's that the cost of a bad idea fell. A lot.

I've watched this in software. When the cost of a deploy drops, teams ship more experiments and more of them fail. That's good, and it looks like chaos from outside.

The same thing is happening in orbit. A payload that would have needed a decade of justification can now ride along on a cheap ride and prove itself or die. I've watched instruments get funded on the strength of one cheap flight.

So the part of the space story I care about isn't the headline launch. It's the number of small things flying and the failure rate that nobody reports. Failure at a low price is how a field learns. Cheap failure. That's the trick.

I don't know which of them matters. Nobody does. That's the point of sending so many.

Our standup went from twenty minutes to seven because somebody finally asked what we were actually trying to learn each morning. Nobody had asked in two years.

The answer was simple. We wanted to know if anybody was stuck and whether any promise we made yesterday was now false. That's it. Once we said it out loud, most of the update became noise.

I cut the format. No status. One question instead. Is anything blocked or about to be. If nothing is, the meeting is ninety seconds and we leave. If something is, we stay until it's unblocked or somebody owns it.

I was worried people would feel out of the loop. The opposite happened, because the information that mattered moved to where it was useful, which was written down, and the meeting stopped being a reading of it.

Xbox cut 3,200 jobs and closed four studios. The reporting put the total at nearly 20,000 across two years. I still don't think the layoffs are the interesting part.

Here's what I keep saying. Nobody at that company decided games were bad. They decided the number was too high. That's a spreadsheet decision, not a taste decision, and it tells you exactly where the pressure came from.

The four studios were Compulsion, Double Fine, Ninja Theory and Undead Labs. Between them they shipped well reviewed games. That's the tell. Quality was not the variable in the room.

So when people argue about whether AI can make good games, I think they're arguing the wrong case. The tool was never on trial. The margin was.

I wrote a post two years ago saying the same thing and I got told I was being cynical. I'm not. Cynical would be saying it doesn't matter. I think it matters a lot, which is why I want the real motive written down instead of the comfortable one. Blame the tool and the spreadsheet wins again.

I run a small open weight model on my own laptop for private work and I'll tell you the trade honestly. I've been doing it for eight months.

It's slower. The context is smaller. The output is worse than the frontier options on anything hard, and I have to think about quantization and memory in a way I never do in the cloud.

I still use it, because the data never leaves the machine and the cost doesn't move when usage does. For anything with a name in it, that trade is worth more to me than a benchmark point.

The part nobody mentions is the maintenance. A local setup is a pet. You update it, you debug it, you own every failure. That's real work and it lands on you at the worst time.

So my advice is to run both and be clear about which is which. Cloud for the hard problems, local for the private ones. And read the license before anything goes near a release.

My first week at a new job taught me more about onboarding than any template, and the lesson was that nobody told me what I was allowed to break. All the docs were there. I read them.

What I couldn't find anywhere was the permission map. Which system can I touch on my second day. Which one needs a second person. Which one will page somebody at two in the morning if I get it wrong.

So I asked, and the answers were interesting. Three of the five systems were fine for a new person. One needed a review and the other needed a ticket and a window. Nobody had written any of that because everybody already knew it.

I wrote it down and put it in the onboarding doc. It's about nine lines. The next hire read it and his first week looked nothing like mine.

New people don't fail because they don't know the architecture. They fail because they don't know where the floors are soft, and that knowledge lives in the heads of whoever's been there longest.

I shipped a fix at six in the evening once and watched the graph for two hours. The morning version of me would have shipped the same fix and slept.

The night version of a decision gets made by somebody who wants to close the laptop, and that person is a poor judge of what a user can tolerate for eight more hours.

I check one thing now before I decide to wait for morning. How many people are affected right now, and is the fix reversible. If it's reversible and somebody is blocked, I ship it. If the change cannot be undone, it waits, and I say out loud why.

I won't ship something irreversible at six because I'm tired of holding it. That's the version of the story where the evening becomes a weekend.

Two rules. One minute of thought. Reversible and urgent goes out. Irreversible waits for daylight and a second pair of eyes.

Four studios shut in one afternoon. All four had shipped something people liked. I want to sit on that fact for a second.

The instinct is to look for the bad game. There isn't one. There's a portfolio review, a target margin, and a list of teams that cost more than the plan allowed.

Everyone tells you to give an AI agent tools. Nobody tells you the part that actually matters, which is what happens when the tool fails.

I've built three small agents now. Each one worked in the demo and broke in the edge, because a tool returning an error is the normal case and not the exception. A model that gets a clean response is easy. A model that has to recover is the whole problem.

So I write the failure path first. What happens when the API times out. What happens when the response is malformed. What happens when the agent loops. If I can't answer those, it doesn't ship. I've held that line three times this year.

I've watched people skip this and I understand the temptation. The happy path is a better video. The failure path is where the thing actually lives, and nobody films it.

Three agents in, my rule is unchanged. No fire and forget. Every call gets a handler or it doesn't get made.

A disk failed on a Friday and the recovery took four hours, and the reason it took four hours is that nobody had ever tested the backup. Four hours. We had three copies and none of them restored.

The backup ran every night and reported success for about two years, and that report only ever meant the copy completed, which is not the same thing as the copy being usable. It never meant anybody could read it. The archive format had changed twice in that window.

One old snapshot saved us. It was on a machine somebody forgot to decommission. We got the data from July and rebuilt the delta by hand, and I spent the weekend not sleeping well.

We restore to a scratch machine every month now. It's scheduled, it has an owner, and the job fails loudly if the restore doesn't open. That's forty minutes of compute a month. Cheapest insurance we have.

A backup you have never restored is a belief system. It's comfortable and it isn't a copy of anything.

Fusion isn't the thing that solves the next five years of demand. It isn't. Anybody selling it that way is selling a story. What it can solve is the part after that. A grid running on batteries covers the evening. It doesn't cover a bad winter or a week of still air, and that's the hole a baseload source fills.

I'd rather argue about the schedule than the magic. Thirty companies with different designs is a portfolio, and a portfolio is the only honest way to bet on something this uncertain. I've no idea which one lands. So would anybody else.

ef6b0a616c5f4158eba79cbec9e2513e77c89fa0.content:
A bug appeared every Tuesday afternoon for four months and the cause was a cron job nobody owned. I want to write down how we found it, because the method is the point.

We couldn't reproduce it. We tried for two weeks and failed, which is the normal outcome when the trigger is time. So we stopped trying to reproduce and started trying to record. Every time it happened we wrote three lines. What the user did, what time it was, what the system said.

After five occurrences the Tuesday pattern was obvious and nobody had seen it, because the reports were spread across a chat and a ticket and two emails. Then it was a thirty minute fix. A cleanup task ran on Tuesdays and deleted rows a report was still reading.

The lesson isn't about cron. It's that the four month cost came from the recording, not the fixing. We had five pieces of evidence and nowhere to put them. If you can't reproduce a bug, stop trying. Start a file. Make the next occurrence write itself down.

A one page document changed a decision I'd been arguing about for three weeks and it took somebody forty minutes to write. One page. Three weeks. I was the one arguing, and I was losing.

1a083118ce2abbf87aa24b8b7fcbd3fa664a0b76.content:
I read the source of a library for the first time in three years and found out I'd been using it wrong. Not badly. Just wrong, in a way the docs allowed.

The function had a default that made it look like it waited. It didn't wait. It returned immediately and the thing I thought was a callback was a timeout handler, so half my calls were racing and I'd been blaming the network. The docs weren't wrong. They were thin.

That's the trade with dependencies. The docs describe intent and the source describes behaviour. When those two differ, the source is the truth and the source is always available. I try to open the source of any package I put on a hot path. Not read all of it. Read the function I call and the one it calls.

Three minutes of reading has saved me two outages this year. The docs were fine both times and I was still wrong.

82e50746e26d9966aa287d93067eb9cfa65b1eb4.content:
A manager told me not now on a project I cared about and it was the right call for reasons he never explained. I spent a month annoyed about the wrong thing. One month.

What I assumed was that he didn't rate the work. What was actually happening was that the team was about to lose two people and he couldn't say so. The project was fine. The timing wasn't.

The part I got wrong was the silence. I treated not now as a verdict on the idea. It was a statement about capacity. I stopped bringing him things for a while and that cost us both.

What I do differently now is ask two questions when I hear not now. Is this a no, or is it a later. And what would have to be true for it to move up. Those two questions have changed about half of those conversations, because most not now answers are about something other than the idea.

Ask what would have to change. If nobody can answer, that's also an answer.

fb69efdeff69a6b9562693668b3da3636e63ec04.content:
I worked with a person who documented nothing for two years and I didn't understand the cost until he left, which turned out to be about four weeks of other people's time.

He was fast. Genuinely fast. His code worked and his reviews were good and he shipped more than anyone. Every one of those things was true right up until his accounts were deactivated. Then the questions started.

Why does this job run at three in the morning. What happens if this queue backs up. Which of these two settings is the real one. Nobody could answer, because the answers lived in his head and he had no reason to write them down. I'm not angry about it. The incentive structure at most companies rewards shipped features and ignores what happens after somebody leaves.

He optimised for the scoreboard he was given. I don't blame him for that. The fix isn't a policy. I ask one question in every review now. If this person is gone next month, what breaks. Then write down the answer. Twenty minutes. It outlives the sprint.

789063f6757a8567ea3b8403b680a4f806fd7280.content:
Everybody asks which model to use. I've started answering with a different question. What happens when it's wrong.

I've built enough with these tools to know the capability isn't the deciding factor. My last three projects all worked in the demo and the difference between them was what they did on a bad day. One failed in the open. One failed in silence. One failed and told me.

The one that told me is still running. The one that failed in silence is the one I had to kill, because a system that's wrong without a signal is worse than a system that's down.

So when somebody asks me for a recommendation I ask about their tolerance instead. What's the cost of a wrong answer, and is there a human in the loop when the cost is high.

I've never once been asked that question back. Not one time in two years. It's the question that decides the answer.

d3e6fb72f4248296d8ae1021a6b77db6b3f07dd8.content:
Our status page said everything was fine for forty minutes while everything wasn't, and the reason was a design decision I made two years earlier.

I'd built it to show the state of the infrastructure rather than the state of the experience. Green meant the servers were responding. Green didn't mean a single user could complete a purchase. The two things diverged in the outage. Every machine was healthy and every request was slow enough that the checkout timed out.

That's the flaw in most status pages. They report the things that are easy to measure rather than the thing the person on the other end is trying to do. It's comfortable to graph a database and it's uncomfortable to define a completed action.

We changed it to one number. Percentage of checkouts completed in the last ten minutes. Everything else moved to a second page. If your status page can be green while your users are angry, you built it for yourself.

I wrote a tool for four months that nobody used and I keep it in a folder because the deletion taught me something. The lesson wasn't about the tool.

It was a local search over our documentation, before the search in the app got good. Mine was faster for power users and slightly worse for everybody else. I built it for the version of the problem I could measure.

The people I made it for needed it to work on a phone, in a meeting, in eight seconds. Mine needed a laptop, a terminal and a config file. I'd measured the search time and never measured the setup time. Nobody told me. They quietly stopped. I found out from a log with four entries in a month. Four entries.

Ask the person who isn't using your thing why. Not the fan. The one who tried it once. The reason is almost never the feature you spent the time on. It's the friction you stopped being able to see because you were the one who set it up.

3e0c2bd38884d49fb098eb0c4481fd96f194abe9.content:
My first on call week taught me that the hardest part is not the fix. It's deciding whether to wake somebody up, and I got that wrong twice.

First time I waited. A graph was ugly and the system was slow and I told myself I'd watch it for another twenty minutes, because I had a theory about a cache warm up and I wanted the graph to prove me right before I involved anybody else at eleven at night. I watched for two hours instead. Then I called, and by then the person I called had twice as much to do.

Second time I called at the first sign and it was nothing. That one felt bad. It was cheaper for everybody. Twenty minutes of somebody's evening against six hours of degraded service.

Our rule is about consequence rather than confidence. If the thing could reach customers within the hour, call. If you'd be embarrassed about waiting another twenty minutes, call. Let the person on the other end decide whether it was worth waking up for. Being wrong in that direction costs minutes and the other direction costs trust.

I don't have a rule that makes this easy. I have a preference about which way I'd rather be wrong.

9b22e20021aa6a2378da608c50d65baf59a71a9b.content:
I sat in a ninety minute meeting last month that should've been a document and I want to describe what the document would've contained. Four paragraphs. That's all.

Paragraph one, the decision we need. Paragraph two, the two options with a cost attached. Paragraph three, what I recommend. Paragraph four, what would change my mind. If those four paragraphs can't be written, the meeting won't produce them either. It'll produce an hour of people talking around a question nobody has stated, and a follow up meeting.

I asked why we met anyway and the answer was alignment. Alignment is a real need and it doesn't require a meeting. It requires that people read before they arrive and that the writer accepts being wrong in public for one day.

I've started writing the four paragraphs and sending them with the invite. Half the time the meeting gets cancelled and the decision happens over replies, which is faster and leaves a record. A meeting is a tool for disagreement. If everybody already agrees, the tool you need is a page.

b04e5a8892dc66a8abcef9979c1f40811bfc0cda.content:
Modding communities keep games alive long after the publisher stops and I've watched that pattern for twenty years.

Here's the thing the industry keeps forgetting. A game with a toolkit gets a decade of new content from people who were never on payroll. A studio gets a reason for the store page to stay warm and the players get something nobody shipped.

I've watched two companies fight this and one embrace it. One embraced it and is still selling copies of a game from a previous console generation. Two fought it and got a modding community anyway, minus the goodwill.

That's the whole analysis. I think the community is coming either way, and the sole choice is whether it has documentation and an official path.

So when I see a roadmap with no toolkit I read it as a bet on a short life. Nothing wrong with that. Just don't act surprised in year three.

I have an old laptop in a drawer that still runs a service for me and I'm not going to replace it. It's been up for eleven months.

It's small. It takes an incoming webhook, stores a row, and sends one message. It runs on a machine most people would call e waste. Eighty lines and it's never needed me.

I'm writing about it because the interesting decision was to not grow it. Every few weeks I think of a feature and then I think about who'd maintain it, and the answer is me, at some point when I'm tired. Most of my worst systems started as something that was correctly small. They got a dashboard and an alert and a config file and then they were a product with one user.

I have one test now and it's about deletion. If this thing disappeared tomorrow, what breaks. If the answer is my own convenience and nothing else, it has permission to stay simple and stay unmonitored.

14f6290f7deca8389668e402b014a66d35ba4e0c.content:
Everybody at my company got AI tools in January and by March the usage numbers told a story nobody wanted to read. Two people used them daily. Most used them twice.

I thought the tools were fine. What was missing was a reason connected to the work somebody already had. The rollout explained the features and never explained which of my four recurring tasks this thing would make shorter.

So the people who adopted it did it because they were curious, and curiosity isn't a strategy. The ones who didn't adopt it weren't resisting. They were busy and the tool arrived as a new thing to learn with no owner.

I found the answer somewhere smaller. One person took the two tasks that annoyed her most and showed four colleagues the prompts she used. That session did more than the training deck.

If you're bringing AI into a team, don't start with what it can do. Start with what somebody already hates doing.

1bf1b82f958119e87462194fd4d0f4379b2fced4.content:
An API I designed in 2022 is still costing people time every week and the flaw is in one field name. That's the whole problem. It's a naming problem. One field.

The field is called status and it holds four different meanings depending on which endpoint you read it from. It means payment state on one route, delivery state on another, and account state on a third. Three meanings. Every client has a comment next to it explaining which one they're getting.

We did that because status was the convenient word on the day each endpoint was written and nobody was looking across them. The cost arrived a year later when a client joined two endpoints together and got a number that meant two different things depending on nothing at all, which is how you find out you named something badly. I can't rename it now. Renaming breaks every client and the field is in a mobile app that a fraction of users never update.

The fix is a new field with a real name and a deprecation window measured in quarters. That's what it costs to be sloppy with a word that felt obvious. Name things for the thing they are, not the thing they're near.

The AI build out is creating a category of job nobody argues about, and it's the electrician rather than the engineer.

I've watched this pattern before. A boom creates demand for the trades two years after it creates demand for the software. Conduit. Cable. Switchgear. Cooling. Four trades, four shortages. Those jobs don't get automated away by the thing they're building.

That's the part of the story I'd tell a young person. The flashy role is crowded and the boring role is short staffed. I've watched two decades of that same mismatch and it never resolves.

So my honest read is that the AI boom is good for the trades and ambiguous for the knowledge work it's named after. Both of those are true and only one gets written about.

I don't know how long the build lasts. Nobody does. I know the wiring outlives the model. Copper lasts decades.

5a863e9db7603bcc76c43d4636a9afccc9fbbc46.content:
A customer told me our product was wrong and he was right and it took me two weeks to admit it. I want to write about the two weeks, because that's the part with the lesson.

My first reaction was technical. He was describing a workflow we didn't support and I explained why the workflow was inefficient. Every sentence I wrote was true and none of it mattered. Not efficiency. He was asking for the thing his team already did.

The second week I did the boring thing. I sat with two of his staff for an hour and watched them work through an order the way they do it every day, and none of it looked like the workflow I'd designed for. They weren't doing it wrong. They were doing it the way their industry does it, and our tool was the thing that was late. We shipped his version four months later and it became the most used part of the product. Nobody had asked for it because nobody had watched.

The customer isn't always right about the fix. He's almost always right about the problem, and the problem is the thing I didn't ask about for two weeks. Watch first.

c135360c19dad44b596738bd6ea40cd19a0803ad.content:
Nobody warns you that the hardest part of shipping a product is answering email. I didn't budget a single hour for it.

The first month I treated support like an interruption to the real work. So replies took two days, and the people writing in got quieter, and I told myself the drop in volume was a drop in problems.

It wasn't. Wrong. Twice wrong. Three of those quiet people had found the same bug and none of them said so twice. I found it four weeks later in the logs. By then my best early user had stopped using the thing.

Now support gets the first hour of my day. Not because it's polite. Because it's the only place where the product's real shape shows up, and the shape in my head hasn't matched the shape in the logs yet.

Turns out the inbox is a research department that pays you in bug reports. Slow replies are how you unsubscribe.

a4b1e7c94e1943b9985340845456b0390c331e83.content:
A test in our suite caught nothing for a year and I only found out because it got deleted by accident. It had passed eleven months of changes that should've broken it.

The test asserted that a function returned a value. That was the whole assertion. Not what the value was. So every regression in the logic walked straight through it while it reported green. That's the failure mode of tests written to raise coverage. They measure that a line ran rather than that a behaviour held, and a line that runs isn't the same as a thing that works.

We rewrote it as four assertions with real data and it failed on the first run, which told us the behaviour had been broken for a while and nobody had noticed because the test was theatre.

Now when a test fails on the first run after being written I don't assume the test is wrong. I assume it found something. A test that can't fail isn't a test. It's a comment that costs compute.

9791efa73991b14f3c7eb706072279523b460275.content:
We have a wiki page about our deployment process that eleven people have bookmarked and nobody has read since March of last year. I know because I checked the revision history.

It's not a bad page. That's the problem. It's a complete page, about two thousand words, and it was correct when it was written and two of the steps have since changed.

What we replaced it with is a script. One command, with the steps as comments, and the script fails if you try to skip a step. Nobody has to read anything because the process is executable now. The wiki page still exists and it links to the script with one sentence about why the script is the source of truth. That's the whole page now.

If a process needs to be read and remembered, it will drift. If it can be run, it stays correct because it's checked by the machine every time somebody uses it.

Always run the process. Never read the process.

435bdf108b59df3fa2eda9467ac094ce9bf97c00.content:
I left a comment in a file four years ago that's still the most useful thing I wrote that year. Three lines. It explains a decision nobody would guess.

I wrote what the code doesn't do and why, with a date and a name. It says the obvious fix is wrong because of a constraint in a system that was retired last spring, which is the kind of thing that takes an hour to rediscover and thirty seconds to write down. That last part is out of date now, and that's fine. An out of date comment that names its date is a gift. It tells you the code is older than the change around it and that somebody thought about it once.

I can't stand comments that describe what the line below does. A loop doesn't need a sentence explaining that it loops. The useful comment is about the road not taken, and there's always one.

Write the why, not the what. One date. One name. Write the thing you had to check twice because it surprised you. Four years later that's the part somebody reads at two in the morning and thanks you for.

Somebody asked me this week why I write about games and fusion and quantum in one feed. I have an answer and it isn't variety.

It's that all of it is the same subject. A tool arrives, the industry argues about taste, the money decides, and the people who made the old thing get repriced. Games, film, energy, war, all of it runs the same script with different nouns.

I noticed that after a few hundred posts and now I can't unsee it. The specific facts change. The structure doesn't. The structure is what I actually write about.

So I read widely on purpose. A fusion funding round and a studio closure teach me the same lesson and I'd miss it if I stayed in one lane.

My advice to anybody building a feed is the opposite of the usual one. Do not narrow down. Find the pattern and let the topics be evidence for it, because the pattern is the thing people can't get anywhere else.

af58b5efdd9ec6d706285fd516099e6ac64ba7c8.content:
A deploy failed on a Sunday because I forgot about a timezone and it took me two hours to see it. Two hours. One line.

The cron expression said midnight. Midnight where. Nobody had asked and I hadn't thought about it, so it ran at midnight on universal time, which was three in the afternoon for the people who read the report. The report was fine. It was just early.

I found it by asking the obvious question, which is where the clock thinks it is. I asked three people before somebody said the server runs on universal time. I'd assumed the machine was local because the meeting was local.

Since then I write the offset into the comment. Not the timezone name. The offset, with a date, because the name changes twice a year and the number doesn't. It takes ten seconds and it has saved me once already, on a Friday night.

6584392c88bdf2a6ae3d6edafed3087be90a6142.content:
I resigned from a job badly once and I've watched other people do it well since, and the difference is one conversation. Talk to your manager before the document.

I sent an email to a calendar invite and let a form do the work. What that produced was two weeks of awkwardness and a manager who found out at the same time as his boss, which made him look bad for no reason.

What the people who do it well do is book thirty minutes first. Thirty minutes. Book it. Not to negotiate. To say the sentence out loud and explain the reason, and to give the manager a chance to ask questions before anybody else knows. Then the process starts. It goes smoothly.

The other thing they do is leave the reason vague in writing. More money, a different problem, a shorter commute. Those are all fine. None of them need detail in a system.

I need these people for references later. The exit's a relationship question, not a paperwork question.

ea3c939131d8294bdaea8e4373151753fd2d255e.content:
I spent three hours reading logs last week and the answer was in the first twenty lines. I want to write about that, because the three hours were my fault and the fix is a habit.

What I did was start at the bottom. That's where the error is. It feels efficient. What happens instead is that you get the symptom and you work backwards through a stack that was already handled.

Read the top first. The first lines tell you what the process was doing when it started, which is usually the context you need. Then I filter for the one word that matters and I look at when it stops appearing, because the last occurrence is where the story turns and everything after it is noise.

The habit now is thirty seconds. Top of the file, before anything else. It feels slow and it isn't. Half the time I know what happened before I have scrolled.

Logs are written in order and I keep reading them backwards.

Depreciation is the word that decides the AI build out and it's the least discussed word in the coverage.

I've watched infrastructure booms get judged on the wrong number. Everyone asks about revenue and nobody asks about the schedule the asset gets written down on. A chip has a short life and a substation has a long one, and those two facts point in different directions.

That's the honest risk. Nobody models it. If the hardware turns over in three years, the build has to earn its money in three years. If the demand forecast is soft in year two, the math stops working and the decision gets made by the lender rather than the operator.

I've watched two of these cycles. In both, the write down came before the write up.

So I'd read the filings rather than the launch events. The useful number is on a line nobody quotes. So I read that line.

b394406a3803b3074c2371069dff10b5069237b1.content:
I rebuilt my local dev environment in about an hour and it fixed a class of bug I had been blaming on production. Nobody warned me about that.

I used the same stack on my laptop for so long that I had stopped noticing the differences. My machine had an older version of one service, a config file that pre dated two changes, and a cache directory that had been growing for a year. All three were invisible because they were always there.

The bug was real on my machine and never happened in staging. So I called it flaky for about four months. What it actually was, was stale.

What I do now is write the setup down in a script and run it from nothing every quarter. New directory, no cache, no reused config. It takes an hour and it has caught four things, two of which were bugs I had been blaming on the network.

Your environment is code. If it isn't reproducible, it's a rumour that you're debugging against.

78bd8fe93e18d344d2618966ffe57541faec3875.content:
The week I noticed burnout I was still shipping. That's what made it hard to see.

Nothing broke. My output was the same on paper. What changed was the Thursday feeling, which I'd started describing as normal, and the fact that I couldn't remember anything I'd decided two days earlier.

What caught it was a note in my own file. I'd written the same blocker three weeks in a row with almost the same words, and the third one had a joke in it. The joke was the tell.

So I took four days off with the laptop in a cupboard. Not a holiday. Just sleep, food, and no decisions. By day three I could read a paragraph and hold it, which sounds small and felt enormous.

I've been back to the edge twice since. Both times the note file caught it earlier, because the pattern is visible in writing and invisible in the day. I don't have a cure. I have a detector, and it cost me nothing to build.
