de559cd59229e82e384cb932c77cd481102599ec.content:
I watched the chip export rules change again in January and most of the coverage was about the wrong country. The interesting question is about the machines, not the chips.

I count a handful of firms that build the equipment for advanced manufacturing. Three companies. They're the actual chokepoint. A chip can be designed anywhere and made in a few places, and none of those places exist without the tools. So the rules that matter name the tools.

What that means practically is that the constraint doesn't move when a design does. A country can have the talent and the money and still be years away, because the machine has to be built and installed and calibrated by people who work for three companies.

I think the second order effect matters more. It pushes effort into manufacturing at older sizes, which is where most of the actual products live. Cars, appliances, industrial gear. Those chips don't need the newest process and they do need capacity.

I follow the tools now, not the chips. Smaller list. It tells you more.

58e1c1cdc00f6a307864b39da811b3b98bc36bb3.content:
I lost a customer last month after two years and the exit call was the most useful forty minutes of my quarter. They didn't churn because of price.

They churned because one workflow needed four manual steps and those four steps never made it onto a roadmap. It was small enough to keep being deprioritised and important enough that a person did it forty times a week.

I got the size of small wrong. A four step workaround done forty times a week. Forty times a week. About six hours of somebody's month, which isn't small from where they're sitting.

We've since added a column to our request list that asks how often a thing happens. Frequency times minutes. It's a rough number and it's changed the order of that list twice. Twice. Frequency times minutes. It works, because the things at the top of that list are not the things we talk about most.

I talk to the ones who leave now. They're the only people with no reason to be polite about it.

76fc3be0573d3c3aeea7ae419c2dd7ed4efcfa1c.content:
Our test suite went from forty seconds to eleven minutes over two years and nobody noticed until a new hire complained on his second day. He was right and we had all adapted.

The tests weren't slow. The setup was. About sixty of them each built the same database fixture from scratch, and each one took about eight seconds because somebody had added a seed step for a feature nobody used.

I found it by timing the setup, not the tests. That's the trick with a slow suite. Everybody profiles the assertions because that's what a test is, and the cost is almost always in what happens before the assertion runs.

We made the fixture once and shared it. Back to about ninety seconds. Eleven minutes of waiting on every push times twenty engineers is the most expensive thing in that repository.

Measure the setup. Nobody does and it's where the time lives.

729af38e6a72c20e8400f0f69b6655ef7b4301c8.content:
I pay attention to who benefits from a story before I decide whether it's true. That habit has saved me more times than any fact check.

The easy version is to call it cynicism. It'sn't. It's just accounting. Every narrative has a beneficiary, and knowing who that's tells you which details got emphasised and which got dropped.

I do this with AI stories and with games stories and with energy stories, and the answer is almost always the same. The person who commissioned the framing is the person whose number improves if you believe it.

That doesn't make the story false. Most distortion is selective rather than invented. Somebody picked which three facts to put in the first paragraph and which twelve to leave out, and the choice was made by a person with a job.

So when I read anything I ask two questions. What does the source want, and what would change my mind. If I can't answer the second one, I'm not reading. I'm being read to.

7c01026c40cf413a62121ed8110cae3d22c89f1a.content:
I wrote a README for a tool last month and it took forty minutes, and the first line did all the work. One sentence about what problem it solves. Not what it is.

Most READMEs open with a description of the software. This is a command line tool that does a thing with files. That's accurate and useless, because I still don't know whether it's for me.

I write one sentence now about the situation you're in when you need it. Then one sentence about what it replaces. Then a command you can paste and run in under a minute, with the output shown so you know what success looks like.

I put the options and the architecture below that. Most people never scroll and that's fine. The people who need the details will find them.

A README isn't documentation. It's the first thirty seconds of a stranger deciding whether to trust you.

36a7e10764541dad5a152738db0fb3b03d9259a6.content:
A robot pilot at a factory near me got covered as a jobs story and most of the coverage skipped the number that matters, which is how many people were on the line before. Nobody said. One number.

The article said twenty five thousand robots over four years. That's a big number and it says nothing about what happens to a specific person. Assembly lines have been automating since before I was born and the pattern is consistent. The task changes first and the headcount changes years later.

What I watch for is whether the company is hiring while it automates. Hiring plus robots is a capacity story and hiring minus robots is a cost story. Those two things have completely different outcomes for the people on the floor and they produce identical headlines.

I'm not against the robots. I'm against reading a number without the direction of the other number next to it.

Two data points, one conclusion. Any story with a single number is a press release.

a3ac71c93f1a9c156a068bec7db2cdcb8f41a0dc.content:
A book changed my mind about something I had believed for fifteen years and it did it with one chapter about a bridge that fell down. Not about software at all.

A bridge failed because a design change was made midway and the people making it didn't go back and redo the calculations. That first design was fine. It looked small. Together they were fatal.

I had believed that a small change doesn't need a full recheck. I believed it because a full recheck is expensive and most of the time the small change is fine. That's how everybody who has ever shipped a bad thing felt right before they shipped it.

Now I ask one question when a small change arrives late. What was this original decision based on and does that still hold. It takes a minute and it has caught two things that would have been quiet and expensive.

It was a book about engineering failures. I took the lesson about process. That's what a good book does.

bc4e8898116de095ad960c9de9c587d7ef243e7b.content:
I've stopped building on top of a single API when I can avoid it and the reason isn't ideology. It's the roadmap.

I've watched two vendors change terms under a product I'd built on. Nothing was promised and nothing was broken. The price moved, the limits moved and one capability got quietly restricted, and the rewrite cost me three weeks.

That's the real lock in. Not the technical dependency. The business dependency. A model you can run yourself is a model nobody can re price without your permission.

So I use both. Hosted for the hard problems, open weights for the parts that have to be mine. The dividing line is simple. If the feature is core, I want a path that doesn't include somebody else's pricing page.

I've made the opposite call plenty of times and paid for it. That's how I learned where the line goes. Money and time.

d715ef3203907904c8ab33d7067e9076cf588486.content:
A support engineer told me something last week that I haven't been able to stop thinking about. She said the bug reports she gets are a map of what our docs fail to explain.

That reframes the whole support queue. I had been reading it as volume. She reads it as feedback about the product, and the pattern she pointed at was obvious once she said it. Six of our top ten tickets were about one setting that had no explanation anywhere.

We didn't need to fix six bugs. We needed to write one paragraph. She had known that for a year and it wasn't her job to act on it.

Since then I've asked her for the top five every month, and the first month we closed three of them with documentation and one with a validation message.

The person closest to the confusion has the clearest view of the fix and the least authority to make it. She was right about all four.

600cc5353b26fea1b3d7eb90d9de7c055d21d579.content:
I watch one number on my own site and it isn't visitors. It's how many people come back a second time.

I know visitors are vanity on paper. What I didn't expect is how much the second visit number tells me about the copy rather than the product. When I rewrote the first paragraph on the landing page, the return rate moved and nothing else changed.

Twelve percent came back the first month. Now it's about thirty, after nine changes and one deletion of a page that was getting lots of traffic and no repeat visits.

That last one hurt. A popular page that people read once and leave is a trap, because it grows a number that feels like progress and produces nothing.

I look at two columns now. New visits, return visits. If the first one climbs and the second one holds, something real is happening. If the first one climbs alone, I've optimised a doorway.
